stem: Young male (around 20) Pt presented after he has a blunt abdominal trauma CT : there was Extravasation around the left kidney What are most appropriate step in management ?
key_concept:
Blunt renal trauma: stability decides, then the type of extravasation.
  • Unstable despite resuscitation: surgical exploration (repair or nephrectomy)
  • Stable + active arterial blush: angioembolization
  • Stable, no active bleeding: non-operative (fluids, observe, serial Hb)
  • Urinary extravasation: mostly observe; ureteric stent if persistent
  • Stable abdominal trauma is imaged with contrast CT
exam_pearl: 'Extravasation' alone does not mean surgery: ask whether it is blood (blush, embolize if stable) or urine (usually observe).

stem: Female pt presented with axillary mass 3x3 on examination the mass was soft and movable Next appropriate step in management
key_concept:
Axillary mass in a woman: image first, biopsy if suspicious, reassure only when clearly benign.
  • Over 30: mammogram ± ultrasound; under 30: ultrasound
  • Suspicious node or solid lesion: core needle biopsy
  • Soft, mobile, rubbery: lipoma or accessory breast tissue likely
  • Hard, fixed, matted: malignancy (breast primary, lymphoma) until proven otherwise
exam_pearl: Soft and mobile lowers suspicion, but a new axillary mass still gets imaging before reassurance.

stem: 32 yo Pregnant women G3P2 at 28 weeks came to the clinic complaining of right breast mass which first noticed 4 months ago, on examination you find round, soft and mobile, movable, right breast mass. No skin change What most appropriate next step or (management?)?
why_right: A breast mass in a pregnant woman (28 weeks) present for 4 months must be evaluated now, and the first and safest imaging in pregnancy is ultrasound. It distinguishes cystic from solid lesions without radiation, and bilateral scanning assesses both breasts and the axillae. A suspicious solid lesion then goes on to core biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mammography is the first choice in a non-pregnant woman over 30; in pregnancy it is not absolutely contraindicated but is less sensitive in dense breasts and needs radiation, so ultrasound comes first.
C. FNA (or core biopsy) follows imaging, not before it; ultrasound first decides whether the mass is a cyst (aspirate) or solid (core biopsy).
D. Deferring until after delivery risks missing pregnancy-associated breast cancer; soft and mobile features are reassuring but a 4-month mass in pregnancy still needs imaging now.
key_concept:
Breast mass in pregnancy: ultrasound first, never wait for delivery.
  • Pregnant or under 30: ultrasound
  • Non-pregnant over 30: diagnostic mammogram ± ultrasound
  • Solid on imaging: core needle biopsy
  • Cystic: FNA
exam_pearl: Benign-feeling mass in pregnancy is still imaged now; 'reassess after delivery' is the trap.

stem: A 32-year-old woman a 28-week pregnant presents with an enlarging right breast mass that has been present for 4 months and is associated with mild pain. Physical examination confirmed a 3 x 2 cm firm movable mass not associated with skin changes or enlarged axillary lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: An enlarging breast mass in a 28-week pregnant woman needs workup now, and the lead-in asks for the next step. Ultrasound is the safest first imaging in pregnancy: no radiation and better than mammography in the dense pregnant breast. Bilateral ultrasound characterizes the 3 x 2 cm mass and checks the other breast and axillae before any biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fine needle aspiration comes after imaging; ultrasound first decides between cyst (aspirate) and solid lesion (core biopsy).
C. Diagnostic mammography would be first in a non-pregnant woman over 30; in pregnancy it is not absolutely contraindicated but ultrasound is done first.
D. An enlarging mass in pregnancy must not be deferred; delay risks missing pregnancy-associated breast cancer.
key_concept:
Breast mass in pregnancy: ultrasound is the first imaging.
  • Pregnant or under 30: ultrasound
  • Non-pregnant over 30: diagnostic mammogram ± ultrasound
  • Solid or suspicious on ultrasound: core needle biopsy
  • Simple cyst: aspiration
exam_pearl: Pregnancy flips the first imaging from mammogram to ultrasound; it never justifies waiting until delivery.

stem: 23 year old presented with abdominal distention and tenderness was diagnosed with bowel obstruction He hax no medical or surgical history What is the cause of the distention ?
why_right: Adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction overall, but they need prior abdominal surgery (or peritoneal inflammation). This 23-year-old has no surgical history (a 'virgin abdomen'), so the most likely cause of his obstruction is a hernia, the commonest cause after adhesions and the leading cause when there has been no previous surgery. Examine the groin and umbilicus for an incarcerated hernia.
why_wrong_block:
B. Adhesions are the top cause of SBO only when there is a history of abdominal surgery (or inflammation such as abdominal TB); here there is none.
C. Meckel's diverticulum can cause obstruction (volvulus, intussusception) in young patients but is much less common than a hernia; it is more typical in children, and often with painless rectal bleeding.
D. This option was not recalled by the source and was described as irrelevant.
key_concept:
Cause of SBO depends on surgical history.
  • Previous abdominal surgery: adhesions
  • No previous surgery (virgin abdomen): hernia (check groin, umbilicus)
  • Large bowel obstruction in older adults: colorectal cancer, then volvulus, diverticular stricture
  • Other SBO causes: Crohn stricture, Meckel's, gallstone ileus, intussusception with a lead point
exam_pearl: 'No surgical history' is the clue that removes adhesions and makes hernia the answer.

stem: Pt present after a MVA with loss of consciousness multiple fracture with sever bleeding and his mouth is full og blood Best way to insure patent airway
key_concept:
Trauma airway: indication to intubate + no major facial injury → endotracheal tube; + facial fracture or failed intubation → cricothyroidotomy.
  • Intubation indications: GCS ≤8 / unconscious, SpO2 <88%, aspiration risk (profuse oral blood or secretions)
  • Facial (mandibular/maxillofacial) fracture + intubation indication → cricothyroidotomy
  • Child <12 y needing surgical airway → needle cricothyroidotomy or tracheostomy
  • Adjuncts (oro/nasopharyngeal airway) are not definitive airways
exam_pearl: "Mouth full of blood" alone means intubate; it becomes cricothyroidotomy only when the stem adds facial or mandibular fractures or failed intubation.

stem: A child (10 y.o) presented to the Emergency department after several hits on his face Intubation was attempted multiple times with failure, What is the best next step in the managment
why_right: This recall's key is tracheostomy because the patient is a child (10 y) with facial trauma and failed repeated intubation, so a surgical airway is needed. Surgical cricothyroidotomy is avoided in children under about 12 years because the cricoid is the narrowest part of the pediatric airway and its injury risks subglottic stenosis, so the surgical airway option left is tracheostomy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Orotracheal intubation has already failed multiple times; repeating it wastes time and causes more trauma. It would be right as the first attempt in a patient needing a definitive airway without a failed attempt.
B. Surgical cricothyrotomy is the rescue airway after failed intubation in adults and older children, but is generally avoided under about 12 years; needle cricothyroidotomy with jet oxygenation is the pediatric emergency bridge.
D. A laryngeal airway (supraglottic device) is a temporary rescue for oxygenation in a failed intubation without major facial disruption; it is not a definitive airway and seats poorly after severe facial trauma.
key_concept:
Failed intubation → surgical airway, chosen by age.
  • Adult / child ≥12 y: surgical cricothyroidotomy
  • Child <12 y: needle cricothyroidotomy as an emergency bridge; avoid surgical cricothyroidotomy
  • Tracheostomy: definitive surgical airway in young children or laryngeal injury
  • Facial fracture + intubation indication in an adult → cricothyroidotomy
exam_pearl: Same stem in an adult flips the answer to cricothyroidotomy; the age (10 years) is what pushes it to tracheostomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler: Answer: C. Traceostomy. Screenshot has red highlights on 'Crico' and 'Trach' as keyword emphasis.

stem: you can examine newborn right reducible inguinal hernia, high raising testies. Left inguinal hernia with no swelling
why_right: A reducible right inguinal hernia in a newborn needs surgical repair by herniotomy (high ligation and excision of the patent processus vaginalis sac). Pediatric inguinal hernias do not close spontaneously and the risk of incarceration is highest in infancy, so repair is done electively soon after diagnosis. The normal left side ("no swelling") needs no treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observation is right for a newborn hydrocele or an umbilical hernia, which usually resolve; an inguinal hernia will not resolve and risks incarceration.
C. Mesh repair is for adult hernias where the posterior wall is weak; in children the defect is a patent processus vaginalis, so sac ligation alone (herniotomy) is enough.
D. Waiting several years applies to pediatric umbilical hernias (most close by 2 years; operate if persistent at 4 to 5 years), not to inguinal hernias, which are repaired promptly.
key_concept:
Pediatric groin/umbilical lumps: who waits and who gets surgery.
  • Inguinal hernia (any age child) → herniotomy, done soon after diagnosis
  • Incarcerated pediatric hernia → attempt reduction, then early herniotomy
  • Umbilical hernia → observe; repair if persistent at 4 to 5 y or large (>2 cm) after 2 to 3 y
  • Hydrocele (transilluminates) → observe until about 1 to 2 y
  • Adult hernia → mesh repair (laparoscopic if bilateral or recurrent)
exam_pearl: Do not confuse the inguinal and umbilical rules: only the umbilical hernia gets years of watchful waiting.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A second restatement in the block (Q: ... 'literally written like that it was confusing', asked about management) with the same options also highlights Herniotomy.

stem: A 34-year-old man fell from the roof of a two-story building. On arrival at the emergency department, he is confused, opens his eyes to sound, and localizes pain with his upper limbs. What is the severity of his brain injury based on the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)?
why_right: Score each component: "opens his eyes to sound" = E3, "confused" = V4, "localizes pain" = M5, giving GCS 12. A GCS of 9 to 12 is a moderate head injury.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mild head injury is GCS 13 to 15; he would need e.g. spontaneous eye opening or obeying commands to reach 13.
C. Severe head injury is GCS 8 or less (the intubation threshold); localizing to pain and verbal confusion keep him well above that.
D. Minimal is not a GCS severity band in the standard mild/moderate/severe classification; where used, it means GCS 15 with no loss of consciousness.
key_concept:
GCS = Eye (4) + Verbal (5) + Motor (6); range 3 to 15.
  • Eye: 4 spontaneous, 3 to speech, 2 to pain, 1 none
  • Verbal: 5 oriented, 4 confused, 3 inappropriate words, 2 incomprehensible sounds, 1 none
  • Motor: 6 obeys, 5 localizes, 4 withdraws, 3 abnormal flexion, 2 extension, 1 none
  • Mild 13 to 15, moderate 9 to 12, severe ≤8
exam_pearl: "Localizes" (M5) and "withdraws" (M4) are the classic trap; one point can move a patient across a band.

stem: Bilateral green discharge recall, there was dilated ducts on mammogram (BI RADS 2) (literally mentioned BIRADS 2), next step?
why_right: Bilateral green (non bloody) nipple discharge with dilated ducts on mammogram fits duct ectasia, a benign condition. The imaging is reported BI-RADS 2 (benign finding), which needs no biopsy, so reassurance with routine follow-up is the next step.
why_wrong_block:
B. Nipple biopsy is for a suspicious nipple lesion such as an eczematous, ulcerated nipple (Paget disease); benign bilateral discharge with BI-RADS 2 imaging does not need tissue diagnosis.
C. CT pelvis has no role in nipple discharge; a pituitary MRI and prolactin, not pelvic CT, would be considered for bilateral milky discharge (galactorrhea).
key_concept:
Nipple discharge: bilateral, multi-duct, non bloody = benign; unilateral, single duct, bloody = investigate.
  • Duct ectasia: greenish discharge, nipple inversion, dilated ducts
  • Intraductal papilloma: commonest cause of bloody discharge
  • BI-RADS 1 to 2 → routine screening; 3 → short interval follow-up; 4 to 5 → core needle biopsy
  • Troublesome duct ectasia or papilloma → duct excision
exam_pearl: Change the discharge to unilateral and bloody, or BI-RADS to 4, and the answer becomes duct excision or core biopsy.

stem: female, recurrent RUQ abdominal pain and diarrhea, RUQ US showed 0.8 polyp, she is bothered by sx, next?
why_right: A gallbladder polyp with recurrent RUQ pain that the patient is "bothered by" is a symptomatic polyp, and gallbladder symptoms that cannot otherwise be explained are an indication for cholecystectomy regardless of polyp size. Surgery treats the symptoms and removes any malignant potential.
why_wrong_block:
B. Conservative management alone suits an asymptomatic small polyp (5 mm or less with no risk factors); this patient is symptomatic.
C. Surveillance ultrasound is right for an asymptomatic polyp of 6 to 9 mm without risk factors (or 5 mm or less with risk factors); symptoms take her out of the surveillance pathway.
D. HIDA scan helps when biliary-type pain has no structural cause on ultrasound (suspected functional gallbladder disorder or acalculous cholecystitis); here a structural lesion is already found and symptoms already justify surgery.
key_concept:
Gallbladder polyp: decide by symptoms, size and risk factors.
  • Symptomatic (unexplained RUQ pain) → cholecystectomy
  • ≥10 mm → cholecystectomy
  • 6 to 9 mm + ≥1 risk factor → cholecystectomy
  • Growth ≥2 mm within 2 years → cholecystectomy
  • 6 to 9 mm no risk factor, or ≤5 mm with risk factor → ultrasound surveillance
exam_pearl: Size rules apply only to asymptomatic polyps; once symptoms are attributable to the gallbladder, operate.

stem: A patient has multiple liver injuries after an accident. What is the management?
key_concept:
Liver trauma: stable → non-operative; unstable → laparotomy with perihepatic packing (damage control). A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Perihepatic packing.
  • Stable, any grade → non-operative management with monitoring
  • Unstable, multiple lacerations → perihepatic packing
  • Packing fails → angioembolization or resection
  • Discrete bleeder → selective vessel ligation
  • Unstable splenic injury → splenectomy
exam_pearl: "Multiple" lacerations point to packing; a single bleeder points to selective ligation.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: An unstable trauma pa7ent has confirmed mul7ple liver lacera7ons. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptD: Individual liga7on of the bleed Pass
why_right: An unstable patient with multiple liver lacerations needs damage control surgery: perihepatic packing compresses the diffuse bleeding quickly, allows resuscitation and correction of coagulopathy, and is followed by a planned second look. If packing fails, angioembolization or resection follows.
why_wrong_block:
A. Right hepatectomy is a long, high-blood-loss operation that an unstable, coagulopathic trauma patient cannot tolerate; resection is reserved for failed packing or later definitive care.
C. Right hepatic artery ligation does not control venous or diffuse parenchymal bleeding from multiple lacerations and risks lobar ischemia; it is a rare last resort.
D. Individual ligation of bleeding vessels suits a single discrete laceration in a patient stable enough for definitive repair, not multiple lacerations in an unstable patient.
key_concept:
Liver injury management is decided by hemodynamics.
  • Stable → non-operative management
  • Unstable → laparotomy + perihepatic packing (damage control)
  • Packing fails → angioembolization or resection
  • Spleen: stable → conservative; unstable → splenectomy
exam_pearl: Make the patient stable and the answer becomes non-operative management, even with multiple lacerations on CT.

stem: An 18-year-old man involved in burn accident, he has 2nd degree burn to his both lower limbs. Weight 70 kg Using Parkland formula, which of the following is most appropriate fluid resuscitation?
OptC: Lactate ringer's 5 L over 1st 6 hrs then 5 L over next 16 hrs
OptD: Lactate ringer's 2.5 L over 1st 6 hrs then 2.5 L over the next 16 hrs
highlight_terms_source: 2nd degree burn to his both lower limbs
why_right: Both lower limbs = 18% + 18% = 36% TBSA (each limb front 9% + back 9%), and second degree (partial thickness) burns count. Parkland: 4 ml × 70 kg × 36 = about 10 L of Ringer's lactate in 24 h, half (about 5 L) in the first part and half over the next 16 h, which matches option C. The formula gives the first half over 8 h from the time of burn; the option prints 6 h, but it is the only one with the correct volumes.
why_wrong_block:
A. 200 ml/hr for 24 h gives only 4.8 L, under half the required 10 L, and ignores front-loading half the volume early.
B. Normal saline bolus then 120 ml/hr is a generic maintenance style regimen, not Parkland: wrong fluid of choice and far too little volume for a 36% burn.
D. A 5 L total corresponds to 18% TBSA; it counts each lower limb as 9% instead of 18%, the classic rule of nines error.
key_concept:
Parkland: 4 ml × kg × %TBSA in 24 h of Ringer's lactate; half in first 8 h (from burn time), half in next 16 h.
  • Rule of nines: each lower limb 18%, each upper limb 9%, head 9%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, perineum 1%
  • Count partial and full thickness burns; exclude superficial (first degree)
  • Monitor by urine output: adult >0.5 ml/kg/hr, child >1 ml/kg/hr
exam_pearl: Each whole lower limb is 18%, not 9%; miscounting it halves the volume (option D).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option C marked with ** and highlighted.

stem: A 24-year-old man recovers from an attack of severe pancreatitis. He has mild epigastric discomfort, sensation of bloating, and loss of appetite. Examination reveals an epigastric fullness .. us : cyst form in lesser sac Diagnosis:
highlight_terms_source: recovers from an attack of severe pancreatitis
why_right: A cyst in the lesser sac appearing after recovery from severe pancreatitis with epigastric fullness, bloating and anorexia is a pancreatic pseudocyst: a fibrous walled fluid collection without epithelial lining that forms more than 4 weeks after acute pancreatitis. CT is the best imaging to confirm it.
why_wrong_block: A. Pancreatic cancer presents in older patients with weight loss and, for head tumours, painless obstructive jaundice; a young man with a lesser sac cyst right after pancreatitis fits a pseudocyst. Other alternatives: pancreatic abscess (fever, leukocytosis, gas on CT) and cystic neoplasm (no pancreatitis history).
key_concept:
Pseudocyst: fluid collection >4 weeks after acute pancreatitis, often in the lesser sac.
  • Presentation: early satiety, epigastric mass or fullness, pain, vomiting
  • Imaging: CT, homogeneous thin walled collection
  • Asymptomatic, <6 cm or <6 weeks → observe
  • >6 cm, >6 weeks, symptomatic or growing → endoscopic internal drainage
  • Infected pseudocyst or abscess → percutaneous drainage
exam_pearl: Add fever, leukocytosis and gas bubbles on CT and the diagnosis becomes pancreatic abscess, treated by percutaneous drainage.

stem: MVA , fractured 3 ribs Patient at first stable Then become distressed Chest clear , :
highlight_terms_source: at first stable Then become distressed
key_concept:
Deterioration after blunt chest trauma: match the sign to the lesion.
  • Paradoxical segment + multiple rib fractures: flail chest (supportive: analgesia, oxygen, ventilation)
  • Hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds + equal air entry: cardiac tamponade
  • Absent breath sounds + hyperresonance + tracheal shift: tension pneumothorax
  • Dull base + absent breath sounds: haemothorax
  • Delayed, progressive hypoxia with a clear chest on auscultation: pulmonary contusion
exam_pearl: Paradoxical movement means flail chest, raised JVP with hypotension and equal air entry means tamponade, and isolated progressive hypoxia means contusion: find the sign before naming the lesion.

stem: A 32-year-old healthy woman had neck ultrasound to evaluate lipoma; incidentally, there was right thyroid lobe 2.3 cm solid hypoechoic nodule (see lab results and report). Test Result Normal Values Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone 2.3 0.4-5.0 pU/mL. Thyroxine (T4 free serum) 11.3 8.5 - 15.2 pmol/L. Fine Needle Aspiration: Follicular neoplasm, Bethesda 4. Which of the following is most appropriate management?
why_right: The decisive clue is the FNA result "follicular neoplasm, Bethesda 4". Cytology cannot separate follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma because that needs capsular or vascular invasion on histology, so the lobe must be removed: hemithyroidectomy (diagnostic lobectomy). The normal TSH and free T4 confirm a non-functioning nodule, so no scan or antithyroid step is needed first.
why_wrong_block:
A. Nodule excision (enucleation) is not an oncological thyroid operation; it leaves uncertain margins and makes later completion surgery harder. Lobectomy is the minimum for a Bethesda 4 lesion.
C. Ultrasound surveillance suits a benign (Bethesda 2) nodule or a nodule below the FNA threshold; it is unsafe for an indeterminate lesion that may be follicular carcinoma.
D. Radiofrequency ablation is for cytologically benign, symptomatic nodules; it destroys tissue and gives no histology, so it is not used for possibly malignant lesions.
key_concept:
Bethesda category decides thyroid nodule management.
  • 1 Nondiagnostic: repeat FNA
  • 2 Benign: ultrasound follow-up
  • 3 AUS/FLUS: repeat FNA
  • 4 Follicular neoplasm: hemithyroidectomy
  • 5 Suspicious for malignancy: manage as 4 or 6
  • 6 Malignant: thyroidectomy (lobectomy or total by size and risk)
exam_pearl: Low TSH with a nodule goes to isotope scan first; normal TSH with Bethesda 4 goes straight to hemithyroidectomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option B marked with ** and highlighted.

stem: RTA case with facial injuries Desaturating Next step?
key_concept:
Trauma airway ladder.
  • Intubation indications: SpO2 below 88%, GCS 8 or less, unconscious, aspiration risk
  • Indication + intact face: endotracheal intubation
  • Indication + major facial or mandibular injury: cricothyroidotomy
  • Nasal adjuncts and nasal tubes: avoid in midface or basal skull fracture
  • Tracheostomy: not the emergency choice in adults
exam_pearl: Facial injury moves the choice to a surgical airway only when it makes oral intubation unsafe or impossible (distorted anatomy, profuse oral bleeding); otherwise intubate.

stem: day 6/7 Post OP (appendectomy i think) fever ,dry wound
why_right: Fever on day 6 to 7 after surgery with a "dry wound" gives no local target: there is no discharge to culture and no collection to open. Among the options, the useful step is to review the drug chart, since drug fever (commonly from antibiotics) is a recognised cause of late postoperative fever when the wound and other sources look clean.
why_wrong_block:
A. A wound swab needs discharge; a dry wound gives nothing to culture. It is right when the wound is red, tender or discharging pus.
B. A throat swab has no role in postoperative fever without sore throat or pharyngitis symptoms.
C. Re-opening the wound treats a wound abscess or infected collection (pain, redness, swelling, pus); with a dry, quiet wound there is no indication.
key_concept:
Postoperative fever by day (the 5 W's).
  • Day 1: atelectasis (wind)
  • Days 2 to 3: pneumonia, UTI (water), superficial thrombophlebitis
  • Days 4 to 5: wound infection, DVT (walking)
  • Day 5 to 7 onward: intra-abdominal abscess, anastomotic leak
  • Any day: drugs (wonder drugs), lines
exam_pearl: After appendectomy a late fever with a clean wound still needs abdominal and DRE examination for a pelvic or intra-abdominal abscess.

stem: A 45-years old female in 5th day post-hysterectomy the patient have fever, she does not complain of anything (Literally Written) and the wound is clean. What is your next step of measurement?
why_right: This recall's key is medication review because the patient is on day 5 with fever but "does not complain of anything" and the "wound is clean": there are no urinary, chest or wound clues to direct tests. Drug fever is a non-invasive, often overlooked cause to check first in an asymptomatic postoperative patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC and blood cultures are right when the patient looks septic (rigors, tachycardia, hypotension) or has a line or clear source; in a well, asymptomatic patient they are not the first step in this recall.
B. Urinalysis and culture is right for fever with urinary symptoms or a catheter, typically on days 2 to 3; here the patient has no complaints.
C. A chest X-ray is right for cough, dyspnoea, crackles or reduced breath sounds, mostly in the first days after surgery (atelectasis, pneumonia); there are no chest findings here.
key_concept:
Asymptomatic postoperative fever: start with the history, examination and drug chart before blind tests.
  • Day 1: atelectasis
  • Days 2 to 3: pneumonia, UTI, thrombophlebitis
  • Days 4 to 5: wound infection, DVT
  • After hysterectomy: also vaginal cuff cellulitis or pelvic collection
  • Drug fever: diagnosis of exclusion; patient often looks well
exam_pearl: Symptoms or signs pointing to a source (dysuria, cough, red wound) move the answer to the matching test.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0599).
Compiler note: 'Q:' recall under 1985 with a different case and options.

stem: A man underwent a sigmoid resection, On postoperative day 4, he develops feve What Is MOST IMPORTANT Thing To Do? (or To Assess) (Not Next, Not Most Appropriate) (Don't Remember The Whole Case But It Was Short And No Exam Findings)
why_right: Fever on "postoperative day 4" falls in the window (days 4 to 5) when surgical site infection is the classic cause, and the lead-in asks for the most important thing to assess. Examining the wound is a bedside step that directly confirms or excludes the commonest cause before any test.
why_wrong_block:
A. A chest X-ray targets atelectasis or pneumonia, which cause fever on day 1 and days 2 to 3, or a patient with chest signs.
B. Blood cultures are right in a septic, unstable patient or with a central line; they come after clinical examination identifies the likely source.
D. Medication review fits a well patient with a clean wound and no source found; it is considered after the wound and abdomen are assessed.
key_concept:
Match the postoperative day to the likely source.
  • Day 1: atelectasis
  • Days 2 to 3: pneumonia, UTI, thrombophlebitis
  • Days 4 to 5: wound infection, DVT
  • After bowel resection, days 5 to 7: anastomotic leak, intra-abdominal abscess
exam_pearl: Day 4 fever: examine the wound first; day 1 to 3 fever: think chest and urine.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with epigastric pain for 6-days, radiating to the back, associated with frequent vomiting. She is known to have multiple small gallstones. Physical examination confirmed diffuse abdominal distention, epigastric tenderness with sluggish bowel sounds (see lab results and report). Test Result Normal Values: Alkaline phosphatase 115 39-117 IU/L; Amylase 149 24-151 IU/L; Direct bilirubin 5.6 1.5-6.5 mol/L; Total bilirubin 15.8 3.5-16.5 mol/L. Erect chest X-ray: Left pleural effusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?
highlight_terms_source: epigastric pain for 6-days, radiating to the back
why_right: This recall's key is urine amylase. Pain for "6 days" radiating to the back, gallstones, ileus (distension, sluggish bowel sounds) and a left pleural effusion suggest acute pancreatitis, but serum amylase (149) is already normal because it falls back within a few days. Urinary amylase stays raised longer, so it is the key's way to confirm a late-presenting pancreatitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Trans-abdominal ultrasound is the initial imaging in acute pancreatitis to look for gallstones; the key rejects it here because the question targets biochemical confirmation of a late presentation with normal serum amylase.
C. CT is reserved for an unclear diagnosis or for severity and complications, ideally after 48 to 72 hours; it is not the initial investigation.
D. Analysis of aspirated gastrointestinal fluid has no diagnostic role in acute pancreatitis.
key_concept:
Acute pancreatitis needs 2 of 3: typical pain, enzymes above 3 times normal, typical imaging.
  • Serum amylase normalises within days; lipase and urinary amylase stay raised longer
  • Ultrasound: look for gallstones (biliary cause)
  • CT: unclear diagnosis or complications, after 48 to 72 hours
  • Left pleural effusion and sentinel loop/ileus support pancreatitis
exam_pearl: A late presenter with normal serum amylase does not exclude pancreatitis; pick the test that stays elevated longer.

stem: A 45-year-old diabetic man underwent a laparotomy for a diverticular perforation. On the 4th post-operative day, he developed a high-grade fever with chills and multiple spikes. On examination, his wound is healthy and his chest is clear to auscultation. On Digital rectal examination, there is bogginess anteriorly. Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 120 /min, Respiratory rate 18 /min, Temperature 38 °C. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
highlight_terms_source: high-grade fever with chills and multiple spikes
why_right: High spiking fever with chills on "day 4" after laparotomy for a perforated diverticulum, with a healthy wound and clear chest, removes wound and chest causes. "Bogginess anteriorly" on DRE localises a pelvic abscess. An established abscess must be drained, so image-guided drainage (with antibiotics as an adjunct) is the treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV antibiotics alone do not clear an established abscess; they are an adjunct to drainage and suit only small collections (under about 4 cm).
B. IV paracetamol only lowers the temperature and does nothing for the pelvic abscess.
C. Abdominal washout (relaparotomy) is for generalised peritonitis, multiple collections, an unstable patient or failed percutaneous drainage; this is a localised collection.
key_concept:
Postoperative intra-abdominal collection: size and stability decide.
  • Small collection: antibiotics
  • Collection of about 4 x 4 cm or more: percutaneous image-guided drainage
  • Multiple collections: laparoscopy
  • Unstable patient or peritonitis: laparotomy
  • Anterior rectal bogginess on DRE = pelvic abscess
exam_pearl: Spiking fever with a clean wound and clear chest after abdominal surgery: do a DRE and look for a pelvic abscess.

stem: A 50-year-old patient underwent a total thyroidectomy 5 hours ago. He has developed a large neck swelling associated with stridor and shortness of breath. Blood pressure 165/90 mmHg, Heart rate 130 /min, Respiratory rate 24 /min, Temperature 37 °C. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A "large neck swelling" with "stridor and shortness of breath" only "5 hours" after total thyroidectomy is a compressive haematoma. The treatment that relieves the airway fastest is opening the skin and strap muscle sutures at the bedside to evacuate the clot, then returning to theatre to control bleeding.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tracheostomy does not remove the compressing clot and is slow through a swollen, distorted neck; evacuation of the haematoma comes first.
B. Close observation is dangerous with stridor; a tense haematoma can obstruct the airway within minutes.
C. Percutaneous drainage fails because a haematoma is clotted blood, and it delays decompression.
key_concept:
Early complications after thyroidectomy.
  • Hours: neck swelling + stridor = haematoma: bedside wound opening
  • Hoarseness, aspiration: recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • Loss of high-pitched voice: superior laryngeal nerve
  • Perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm: hypocalcaemia (check calcium)
  • Refractory hypocalcaemia: check magnesium
exam_pearl: Swelling plus stridor within hours of thyroid surgery means open the wound now, not intubate or scan first.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe abdominal pain and absolute constipation for 2 days associated with nausea and vomiting. He has a significant past history of constipation requiring use of laxatives. On examination, his abdomen is distended, tense, tender all over with a palpable mass in the left lumbar and hypochondrium (see image). Which of the following is the most likely site of volvulus?
why_right: Pain, "absolute constipation" and vomiting with a distended tense abdomen mean large bowel obstruction. The "long history of constipation requiring laxatives" (elongated, redundant sigmoid) and a "mass in the left lumbar and hypochondrium" (the twisted, dilated loop) point to sigmoid volvulus, the commonest colonic volvulus.
why_wrong_block:
A. Caecal volvulus occurs in younger patients with a congenitally mobile caecum, without the long laxative history; the dilated caecum often moves toward the epigastrium or left upper abdomen with small bowel dilatation, so the chronic constipation is the decisive clue against it.
B. The rectum is fixed in the pelvis without a mobile mesentery, so it does not twist.
D. Transverse colon volvulus is very rare and would give a central or upper abdominal mass rather than a left-sided mass with chronic constipation.
key_concept:
Colonic volvulus: site by clue.
  • Sigmoid: elderly, chronic constipation, laxatives, institutionalised; left-sided mass; coffee bean loop pointing to RUQ
  • Caecum: younger, mobile caecum; dilated caecum displaced toward LUQ or epigastrium, small bowel dilated
  • Stable sigmoid volvulus: endoscopic (sigmoidoscopic) decompression
  • Ischaemia, perforation or peritonitis: sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy
exam_pearl: Chronic constipation on laxatives in an older patient is the clue for sigmoid; a twisted caecum can also end up on the left, so the side of the mass alone can mislead.

stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C and liver cirrhosis presented to Emergency Room with perforated peptic ulcer that requires urgent laparotomy (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values: Hb 90 130-170 g/L (Male) - 120-160 g/L (Female); Platelets count 90 150-400 x 109/L; INR 2 0.8-1.2; Prothrombin time 17 10-13 sec. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management prior to the procedure?
why_right: This cirrhotic patient needs an urgent laparotomy and his main correctable defect is the coagulopathy: INR 2 and PT 17 reflect poor hepatic synthesis of clotting factors. Fresh frozen plasma replaces the whole range of clotting factors, so it is the most appropriate product to give before the procedure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Platelets: the count of 90 is low but well above the level usually needed for major surgery (around 50); platelets are given when the count is below that or there is platelet dysfunction.
B. Cryoprecipitate: mainly supplies fibrinogen (plus factor VIII and vWF); it is right for low fibrinogen or DIC, not for a raised INR from global factor deficiency.
D. Packed red blood cells: Hb 90 is above the usual restrictive threshold of 70 in a stable patient and does not correct bleeding risk; give RBCs for active major bleeding or Hb below threshold.
key_concept:
Match the blood product to the defect.
  • High PT/INR (factor deficiency, cirrhosis, urgent surgery): FFP
  • Warfarin reversal with bleeding: vitamin K IV plus PCC or FFP
  • Low fibrinogen / DIC: cryoprecipitate
  • Low platelets for major surgery or bleeding: platelets
  • Low Hb or active hemorrhage: packed RBCs
exam_pearl: In cirrhosis the abnormal number to fix before urgent surgery is the INR, not a mildly low platelet count or Hb.

stem: A 65-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of vague upper abdominal pain associated with progressive yellowish discoloration of his sclera, dark urine and weight loss. On examination, he was jaundiced with a palpable, distended non-tender gallbladder (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values: Alkaline phosphatase 320 39-117 IU/L; Direct bilirubin 77 1.5-6.5 mol/L; Total bilirubin 88 3.5-16.5 mol/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Progressive jaundice with only vague pain, dark urine and weight loss over 3 months in a 65-year-old point to malignant obstruction. A palpable, distended, non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) means the block is distal to the cystic duct junction, which is the territory of a periampullary tumour (pancreatic head, ampulla, distal CBD, duodenum).
why_wrong_block:
A. Klatskin tumour: obstructs at the hilum above the cystic duct, so the gallbladder is collapsed and not palpable; right when US shows only intrahepatic dilatation with a shrunken gallbladder.
C. Common bile duct stone: the gallbladder is usually chronically inflamed and fibrosed so it does not distend, and jaundice tends to fluctuate with pain; right in fluctuating jaundice with biliary colic or cholangitis.
D. Hepatocellular carcinoma: causes a hepatocellular or mixed picture in a cirrhotic liver, not a distended gallbladder; think of it with cirrhosis, hepatomegaly and raised AFP.
key_concept:
Gallbladder state localises the biliary block.
  • Distended, non-tender, palpable (Courvoisier): distal block, periampullary or pancreatic head cancer
  • Collapsed gallbladder with intrahepatic dilatation only: hilar block, Klatskin tumour
  • Fluctuating jaundice with colic: CBD stone
  • Weight loss plus progressive jaundice: malignancy until proven otherwise
exam_pearl: Courvoisier sign = jaundice + palpable non-tender gallbladder, which is unlikely to be stones.

stem: A 67-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of yellowish discoloration of his sclera and skin with dark urine and pale stool. On examination, he was jaundiced with a palpable distended gallbladder (see report and lab results). Test Result Normal Values: Alkaline phosphatase 421 39-117 IU/L; Direct bilirubin 122.3 1.5-6.5 mol/L; Total bilirubin 134.5 3.5-16.5 umol/L. Ultrasound: Dilated intra and extrahepatic bile ducts with hugely distended gallbladder. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Dilated intra and extrahepatic bile ducts with hugely distended gallbladder
why_right: Jaundice with dark urine and pale stool plus very high ALP and direct bilirubin is obstructive jaundice. The palpable distended gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) and US showing dilated intra- AND extrahepatic ducts with a hugely distended gallbladder put the block at the distal CBD, classically from pancreatic head cancer in an older man.
why_wrong_block:
A. Klatskin tumour: a hilar block gives intrahepatic dilatation only with a collapsed gallbladder; here the extrahepatic ducts and gallbladder are distended.
C. Mirizzi's syndrome: a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck compresses the common hepatic duct, usually with a contracted, inflamed gallbladder and pain; right in a gallstone patient with dilatation above the cystic duct level only.
D. Common bile duct stone: can dilate both duct systems, but the scarred stone-bearing gallbladder rarely distends and jaundice is usually painful and fluctuating.
key_concept:
Level of obstruction on US.
  • Intra + extrahepatic dilatation, big gallbladder: distal CBD, pancreatic head / periampullary tumour
  • Intrahepatic only, collapsed gallbladder: hilum, Klatskin tumour
  • Gallbladder neck stone compressing CHD: Mirizzi syndrome
exam_pearl: A hugely distended gallbladder with painless obstructive jaundice argues against stones and for a distal malignancy.

stem: A 74-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of vague upper abdominal pain associated with progressive yellowish discoloration of his skin and sclera and dark urine. On examination, he was jaundiced (see lab result and report). Test Result Normal Values Alkaline phosphatase 312 39-117 IU/L Direct bilirubin 87 1.5-6.5 mol/L Total bilirubin 97 3.5-16.5 mol/L Ultrasound: Dilated intrahepatic biliary tree with collapsed gallbladder. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Progressive obstructive jaundice (dark urine, high ALP and direct bilirubin) in a 74-year-old with US showing dilated intrahepatic biliary tree and a collapsed gallbladder puts the block at the hepatic duct confluence, above the cystic duct. Bile cannot reach the gallbladder, so it stays empty: this is a Klatskin tumour (hilar cholangiocarcinoma).
why_wrong_block:
B. Mirizzi's syndrome: due to a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck, so the gallbladder contains stones and is inflamed with RUQ pain; right in a gallstone patient with CHD compression.
C. Gallbladder cancer: shows a gallbladder mass or wall thickening, often with gallstones, rather than a simply collapsed empty gallbladder.
D. Periampullary tumour: a distal block dilates both intra- and extrahepatic ducts and distends the gallbladder (Courvoisier).
key_concept:
Collapsed gallbladder + intrahepatic dilatation only = obstruction above the cystic duct.
  • Klatskin: hilar, collapsed gallbladder
  • Periampullary / pancreatic head: distal, distended gallbladder, both duct systems dilated
  • Mirizzi: stone in gallbladder neck compressing CHD
exam_pearl: Do not choose periampullary just because the patient is old with jaundice; the collapsed gallbladder is the decisive clue.

stem: The vascular surgeon was called for help in the Operating Room by the colorectal surgeon who is doing a low anterior resection for colon cancer as he encountered pelvic bleeding that he could not control. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: Uncontrollable pelvic bleeding during a low anterior resection is classically from the presacral venous plexus or pelvic vessels in a deep, narrow field. The first move is heavy packing of the pelvis with direct pressure, which tamponades venous bleeding, buys time for the anaesthetist to resuscitate, and lets the team regroup before any further step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Do on table angiogram: takes time and needs a stable patient; angiography and embolisation are for persistent arterial bleeding after temporary control.
C. Infra renal aortic clamp: does not control venous plexus bleeding and is not the first step; aortic clamping is reserved for failure of packing with ongoing haemorrhage.
D. Supra celiac aortic clamp: a rescue step when the patient becomes profoundly hypotensive despite packing (the follow-up scenario), not the initial manoeuvre.
key_concept:
Ladder for uncontrolled intraoperative pelvic bleeding.
  • Step 1: pack the pelvis with pressure and resuscitate
  • Packing fails with profound hypotension: supraceliac aortic clamp
  • Then definitive control once resuscitated (repair, ligation, embolisation, or damage control)
exam_pearl: Pressure and packing first; clamps and angiography come only when packing fails.

stem: The vascular surgeon was called for help in the Operating Room by the colorectal surgeon who is doing a low anterior resection for colon cancer as he encountered pelvic bleeding that he could not control, the pelvis was packed and the bleeding slowed down but the patient dropped his pressure again. Blood pressure 60/40 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
OptD: Remove the packs and repair the injury
why_right: The pelvis has already been packed, yet the patient has dropped his pressure again to 60/40, meaning ongoing life-threatening haemorrhage. The key here is a supraceliac aortic clamp: it can be applied quickly at the diaphragmatic hiatus away from the bloody pelvic field, controls all aortic inflow and maintains perfusion to the heart and brain while resuscitation catches up and definitive control is planned.
why_wrong_block:
A. Do on table angiogram: too slow for a patient at 60/40; angiography and embolisation suit a patient stable enough to wait.
B. Infra renal aortic clamp: needs dissection close to the retroperitoneal and pelvic haematoma and gives less proximal control; it is used for elective aortic work or bleeding with time to expose the infrarenal aorta.
D. Remove the packs and repair the injury: removing packs in a hypotensive patient restarts uncontrolled bleeding; repair comes after inflow control and resuscitation.
key_concept:
Pelvic bleeding during LAR, stepwise.
  • First: heavy pelvic packing
  • Packing in place but BP crashes (60/40): supraceliac aortic clamp
  • Then resuscitate and achieve definitive control
exam_pearl: Note the twist from the first version of this case: packing done and still hypotensive switches the answer from packing to supraceliac clamping.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked with ** in the screenshot; 'Infra' and 'Supra' highlighted in red for contrast.

stem: A 37-year-old complained of a right breast lump for 3 months. She has family history of breast cancer. Physical examination confirmed a hard lump in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast with ill-defined edge and skin tethering and no palpable axillary lymph node. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A 37-year-old with a family history and a hard, ill-defined lump with skin tethering needs triple assessment, and in a woman older than 30 the next step is imaging: bilateral mammography (with or without ultrasound). Imaging comes before biopsy so the lesion is characterised and the other breast is screened, and the biopsy then targets the lesion without distorting the images.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI breast: a problem-solving or high-risk screening tool (e.g. known BRCA, dense breasts, occult primary), not the first test for a palpable lump.
B. Core needle biopsy: the definitive tissue diagnosis and the step after imaging; it becomes the answer once mammography or US shows a suspicious (BI-RADS 4 or 5) lesion.
D. Fine needle aspiration cytology: gives cytology only, cannot distinguish invasive from in situ disease or give receptor status; core biopsy has replaced it for solid lumps.
key_concept:
Breast lump workup = triple assessment: exam, imaging, biopsy.
  • Age under 30: ultrasound first
  • Age 30 or more: mammography with or without ultrasound
  • Suspicious imaging (BI-RADS 4/5): core needle biopsy
  • MRI: selected high-risk or problem-solving cases
exam_pearl: Malignant-sounding features tempt you to jump to biopsy, but the first step at 30 or older is still mammography.

stem: A 33-year-old man was involved in a motor vehicle crash. On arrival to the Emergency Department, he was conscious and alert. Examination showed an open wound to the anterior surface of the neck with devitalized tissue. Blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, Heart rate 104 /min, Respiratory rate 28 /min, Oxygen saturation 87%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: open wound to the anterior surface of the neck
why_right: Airway comes first. This patient has an open anterior neck wound with devitalized tissue, is tachypnoeic (RR 28) and hypoxic at SpO2 87%; saturation below 88% is an indication for a definitive airway. While he is still conscious, endotracheal intubation secures the airway before swelling or haematoma make it impossible.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxygen mask: adequate for a hypoxic trauma patient with a protected airway, but here the airway is threatened by the neck wound and saturation is already below 88%.
B. Tracheostomy: a formal, slower surgical airway for elective or semi-elective settings, not the emergency step.
C. Cricothyroidotomy: the emergency surgical airway when intubation fails or is impossible (severe maxillofacial trauma, cannot intubate cannot oxygenate).
key_concept:
Trauma indications for a definitive airway (intubation).
  • SpO2 below 88% despite oxygen
  • GCS 8 or less / unconscious
  • Risk of aspiration (oral bleeding, secretions)
  • Threatened airway: neck wound, expanding haematoma, burns
  • Intubation fails or impossible: cricothyroidotomy
exam_pearl: Conscious and alert does not mean a safe airway; hypoxia plus a neck wound means intubate now.

stem: A 25-year-old man brought to the Emergency Department after he was involved in motor vehicle crash, which was driving at a speed of 130 km/hour. Patient was wearing seat belt. On arrival to the Emergency Department, he was conscious, and alert (see report). Chest X-ray: Normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: High-speed blunt trauma (130 km/h) warrants abdominal imaging, and this patient is conscious and alert, i.e. treated as haemodynamically stable, with a normal chest X-ray. The stable blunt abdominal trauma patient goes for CT abdomen (with contrast), which grades solid organ injury and detects hollow viscus and retroperitoneal injury.
why_wrong_block:
A. US abdomen (FAST): the bedside test for the unstable patient to look for free fluid; it misses many solid organ, bowel and retroperitoneal injuries.
C. Diagnostic laparoscopy: used mainly for suspected diaphragmatic injury or equivocal penetrating trauma in a stable patient, not as first evaluation.
D. Exploratory laparotomy: for unstable patients with positive FAST, peritonitis, evisceration or gunshot wounds, none of which is present.
key_concept:
Abdominal trauma triage by stability.
  • Stable: CT abdomen
  • Unstable blunt: FAST; positive leads to laparotomy
  • Peritonitis, evisceration or unstable with free fluid: laparotomy
exam_pearl: Stability decides the test: stable goes to CT, unstable gets FAST.

stem: 9 year old girl suspected of appendicitis(they stated that), complain of right lower quadrant pain, no fever no anorexia and no rebound tenderness WBC 9 What is the best thing to do to avoid missing the diagnosis?
OptA: Admit and do serial examination and repeat lap in 6-12 hrs
OptC: Discharge patient with given instructions when to come back
highlight_terms_source: no fever no anorexia and no rebound tenderness
why_right: This 9-year-old has RLQ pain only, with no fever, no anorexia, no rebound and a normal WBC of 9: a low-probability picture for appendicitis. The safest way to avoid missing an evolving appendicitis is active observation: admit, repeat the abdominal examination and repeat the labs over 6 to 12 hours, so that the signs declare themselves without exposing the child to unnecessary radiation or surgery.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT: avoided in children because of radiation; when imaging is needed in a child, ultrasound is first line, and CT is kept for equivocal cases or complications such as abscess.
C. Discharge patient with given instructions: reasonable only for a very low-risk patient with reliable follow-up, but the question asks how to avoid missing the diagnosis, which needs in-hospital serial assessment.
key_concept:
Suspected appendicitis: act on the probability.
  • Low probability (no fever, no rebound, normal WBC): admit, serial exam and repeat labs
  • Equivocal, child or pregnant: ultrasound first
  • Equivocal adult or obese adult: CT
  • High probability (classic picture, rebound, leukocytosis): appendectomy
exam_pearl: Normal WBC and no peritonism do not exclude early appendicitis; serial examination is the safety net.

stem: Patient with resistant hypertension associated with palpitations, sweating, and headaches. Most definitive treatment?
why_right: "Resistant hypertension" with the triad of palpitations, sweating and headaches is the classic picture of pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine secreting adrenal tumour. The lead-in asks for the most definitive treatment: surgical removal of the tumour (adrenalectomy, usually laparoscopic) is the only cure. It is done after preoperative alpha blockade (e.g. phenoxybenzamine), with a beta blocker added only once alpha blockade is established.
why_wrong_block: A. Renal artery stenting treats renovascular hypertension (renal artery stenosis: resistant hypertension, abdominal bruit, asymmetrical kidneys, rise in creatinine on ACE inhibitor). It does not explain episodic adrenergic symptoms like sweating and palpitations.
key_concept:
Pheochromocytoma: triad of headache, sweating, palpitations with (paroxysmal or resistant) hypertension.
  • Diagnosis: plasma free or 24 h urine metanephrines/catecholamines, then CT/MRI adrenal
  • Initial BP control: alpha blocker (phenoxybenzamine) first
  • Beta blocker only after alpha blockade (risk of unopposed alpha crisis)
  • Definitive: adrenalectomy
  • Renal artery stenosis: bruit, small kidney, no adrenergic spells → angioplasty/stenting
exam_pearl: "Initial / control BP" = alpha blocker; "definitive / cure" = adrenalectomy; a beta blocker first is the classic wrong answer.

stem: Patient with bowel obstruction. Most appropriate investigation?
why_right: The lead-in is "most appropriate investigation" for bowel obstruction, not the initial one. CT abdomen with contrast is the confirmatory test: it confirms obstruction, finds the transition point and cause (adhesion, hernia, tumour, volvulus) and detects strangulation or ischemia that would need urgent surgery. Plain X-ray is only the first screening film.
why_wrong_block:
A. Abdominal X-ray is the initial test (dilated loops, air-fluid levels) but it cannot show the cause or ischemia; it is the answer when the question says "best initial".
B. Ultrasound is limited by gas-filled bowel in adults; it is the first choice in young children (intussusception) or pregnancy.
D. Colonoscopy is not used to diagnose acute obstruction (insufflation risks perforation); it is used later, e.g. to evaluate a suspected colonic tumour or to decompress sigmoid volvulus.
key_concept:
Bowel obstruction imaging ladder:
  • Initial: erect CXR (free air) + supine/upright abdominal X-ray
  • Confirmatory/most appropriate: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
  • Child with suspected intussusception: ultrasound first
  • Peritonitis or strangulation: laparotomy, do not delay for imaging
exam_pearl: "Initial" = X-ray; "most appropriate/confirm/cause" = CT with contrast.

stem: Patient with bowel obstruction. Best initial investigation?
why_right: The lead-in is "best initial investigation". Plain abdominal X-ray (supine and upright, with an erect chest X-ray for free air) is cheap, fast and shows dilated loops and air-fluid levels, so it is the first test in suspected bowel obstruction. CT then follows to confirm the cause and look for complications.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT abdomen is the confirmatory, most informative test; it is the answer when the question asks "most appropriate" or "confirm", not "initial".
C. Ultrasound is poor in adults because bowel gas blocks the view; it is the initial test in toddlers (intussusception) or pregnancy.
key_concept:
Initial vs confirmatory in bowel obstruction:
  • Initial: abdominal X-ray + erect CXR
  • Confirmatory: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast
  • SBO on X-ray: central dilated loops with valvulae conniventes
  • LBO on X-ray: peripheral dilated colon with haustra
  • Child: ultrasound first
exam_pearl: Same disease, different verb: "best initial" = X-ray, "most appropriate" = CT.

stem: Female in her 50s or 70s with localized LLQ tenderness and pain. Most appropriate investigation?
why_right: An older woman ("50s or 70s") with localized LLQ tenderness and pain is acute diverticulitis until proven otherwise. CT abdomen with contrast is the investigation of choice: it confirms the diagnosis and shows complications such as abscess or perforation, which decide management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colonoscopy is avoided in acute diverticulitis (perforation risk); it is done 6 to 8 weeks after recovery to exclude colon cancer.
C. Plain X-ray only shows free air or obstruction; it cannot diagnose diverticulitis or its abscess.
D. Ultrasound is operator dependent and less accurate for diverticulitis; it is preferred for gynecologic causes, pregnancy or children.
key_concept:
Diverticulitis: older patient + LLQ pain/tenderness ± fever, change in bowel habit.
  • Investigation of choice: CT abdomen with contrast
  • Uncomplicated: antibiotics/supportive care
  • Abscess: percutaneous (image guided) drainage
  • Perforation with peritonitis: laparotomy
  • Colonoscopy 6 to 8 weeks after the attack
exam_pearl: Colonoscopy is right only AFTER the attack settles; during the acute attack the answer is CT.

stem: Female with rapidly enlarging 5 cm breast mass. Biopsy showed stromal cells with increased mitotic figures. Diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: stromal cells with increased mitotic figures
key_concept:
Fibroadenoma vs phyllodes vs carcinoma:
  • Fibroadenoma: young, small, slow growth, bland stroma
  • Phyllodes: rapid growth, large, cellular stroma with mitoses, leaf-like pattern
  • Phyllodes spreads hematogenously, not to axillary nodes
  • Phyllodes treatment: wide local excision with at least 1 cm margins; mastectomy if very large
  • Carcinoma: malignant epithelial cells, older age, fixed hard mass
exam_pearl: "Stromal" + "mitoses" + "rapidly enlarging" are phyllodes words; carcinoma is defined by abnormal epithelial cells.

stem: Female with long history of autoimmune thyroiditis developed thyroid malignancy. Most likely type?
why_right: A long history of autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis is the classic risk factor for primary thyroid lymphoma (usually B-cell non-Hodgkin), which arises from the chronic lymphocytic infiltrate of the gland. Hashimoto carries a markedly increased relative risk of lymphoma, so this is the expected exam association.
why_wrong_block:
A. Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer overall and is also linked to Hashimoto, but it is the second association taught; it is the answer when the stem gives radiation exposure, a solitary nodule with lymph node spread, or psammoma bodies.
B. Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, is linked to MEN 2/RET mutation and raised calcitonin, not to autoimmune thyroiditis.
C. Anaplastic carcinoma is a rapidly growing tumour of elderly patients, often arising from long-standing goiter or differentiated cancer; it has no specific link to Hashimoto.
key_concept:
Thyroid cancer association map:
  • Hashimoto → lymphoma (classic), then papillary
  • Radiation, lymphatic spread → papillary
  • Hematogenous spread (bone, lung, liver) → follicular
  • Calcitonin, MEN 2 → medullary
  • Elderly, rapid hard mass, poor prognosis → anaplastic
exam_pearl: Hashimoto + rapid enlargement (± B symptoms) = lymphoma; Hashimoto alone can still tempt you toward papillary.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a progressive anterior neck swelling with stridor. She has a 12-year history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Physical examination confirmed a diffuse, large, non-tender thyroid swelling with retrosternal extension. A core needle biopsy was ordered (see reports). Ultrasound: Diffuse thyroid enlargement, encasing bilateral carotid sheaths. Histopathology: Malignant thyroid tumour. Which of the following is the most likely tumour?
highlight_terms_source: progressive anterior neck swelling with stridor
why_right: A woman with a 12-year history of Hashimoto thyroiditis now has a 3-month progressive, diffuse goiter with stridor, retrosternal extension and encasement of both carotid sheaths, and the biopsy is malignant. Rapid diffuse enlargement in a long-standing Hashimoto gland is the classic presentation of primary thyroid lymphoma, the malignancy most strongly associated with autoimmune thyroiditis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Follicular carcinoma presents as a solitary nodule in a normal-sized gland and spreads hematogenously (bone, lung); it does not cause rapid diffuse enlargement in a Hashimoto gland.
B. Medullary carcinoma is a C-cell tumour with raised calcitonin and MEN 2 links, usually a nodule rather than a diffuse goiter.
C. Anaplastic carcinoma also grows fast with compressive symptoms, but it typically affects elderly patients with a long-standing goiter and is a hard, fixed mass; the Hashimoto background points to lymphoma instead.
key_concept:
Rapidly growing thyroid mass with compression:
  • Background Hashimoto, diffuse enlargement → lymphoma (core biopsy, chemotherapy ± radiotherapy)
  • Elderly, long-standing goiter, hard fixed mass → anaplastic
  • Lymphoma is very responsive to treatment, anaplastic has very poor prognosis
exam_pearl: Rapid growth alone points to both lymphoma and anaplastic; the Hashimoto history is the tie-breaker for lymphoma.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presented with a recent rapid enlargement of a neck swelling associated with weight loss. She was diagnosed 25 years ago with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis diagnosed 25 years ago now has recent rapid enlargement of the neck swelling with weight loss (a B symptom). Long-standing autoimmune thyroiditis plus rapid growth and constitutional symptoms is the textbook picture of primary thyroid lymphoma.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hemorrhagic goiter (bleed into a nodule or cyst) causes sudden, often painful enlargement over hours to days, without weight loss or a link to Hashimoto.
C. Papillary carcinoma is usually a slow-growing nodule ± cervical nodes; rapid diffuse growth with B symptoms is not its typical course.
D. Subacute thyroiditis presents with a painful, tender gland after a viral illness, fever, transient hyperthyroidism and raised ESR; it is not linked to long-standing Hashimoto or weight loss from malignancy.
key_concept:
Neck swelling in a patient with Hashimoto:
  • Rapid enlargement + B symptoms (weight loss, fever, night sweats) → thyroid lymphoma
  • Sudden painful swelling over hours → hemorrhage into a nodule
  • Painful tender gland after URTI, high ESR → subacute thyroiditis
  • Diagnosis of lymphoma: core or open biopsy (FNA often insufficient)
exam_pearl: Weight loss in a long-standing Hashimoto patient with a growing goiter = lymphoma, not just a bigger goiter.

stem: Patient with ruptured appendix and localized abscess. Most appropriate management?
why_right: A ruptured appendix that has walled off into a localized abscess is managed non-operatively first: percutaneous image-guided drainage plus IV antibiotics, then interval appendectomy after the inflammation settles. Operating immediately on an inflamed, matted abscess has higher complication rates (bowel injury, ileocecal resection), which is why surgery is delayed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Immediate appendectomy is right for uncomplicated appendicitis or for free perforation with generalized peritonitis; with a contained abscess it risks a difficult, morbid operation.
C. Antibiotics and observation alone fit an appendiceal phlegmon (inflammatory mass without pus). A localized abscess needs the pus drained, and the classic plan then removes the appendix later because the abscess can recur and, in older patients, an underlying appendiceal or cecal tumour must be excluded.
key_concept:
Appendicitis by stage:
  • Uncomplicated: laparoscopic appendectomy
  • Phlegmon (mass, no pus): IV antibiotics, conservative
  • Abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics → interval appendectomy
  • Free perforation with generalized peritonitis: urgent appendectomy + washout
exam_pearl: Localized abscess = drain now, operate later; generalized peritonitis = operate now.

stem: Patient complaining of perianal painful lump for 12 hours. 1*1 in size, Dome shaped, Bluish in color and tender. Management?
why_right: A painful, tender, dome-shaped, bluish perianal lump of 12 hours is an acutely thrombosed external hemorrhoid. This recall's key is lateral internal sphincterotomy, reasoning that internal sphincter spasm drives the pain and venous congestion, so lowering the high anal resting pressure treats the cause. It is kept here as keyed; see the concern note.
why_wrong_block:
A. Conservative care (sitz baths, analgesia, stool softeners, topical agents) is the usual choice when a thrombosed external hemorrhoid presents after about 72 hours, when the pain is already settling.
B. Rubber band ligation is for grade I to III internal hemorrhoids above the dentate line; banding the somatically innervated external tissue causes severe pain.
D. Needle aspiration does not evacuate the clotted thrombus and is not a standard option; when early intervention is chosen it is excision (or incision and evacuation) of the clot.
key_concept:
Painful perianal lump:
  • Thrombosed external hemorrhoid: acute, tender, bluish/purplish lump
  • Within about 72 h: excision of the thrombosed hemorrhoid under local anesthesia
  • After about 72 h: conservative
  • Lateral internal sphincterotomy: standard surgery for CHRONIC anal fissure
  • Perianal abscess: red, fluctuant, fever → incision and drainage
exam_pearl: Bluish tender lump with acute pain is a thrombosed hemorrhoid, not a fissure; sphincterotomy is the textbook fissure operation.

Most likely diagnosis/management?' A. Conservative management B. Aspiration C. Band ligation (no answer marked in typed block). Screenshot (fuller recall, used as stem) note (Arabic): answer C, memorize it; a surgeon asked and C was correct. 'Smle by hamza answered C and he got 100. Alharbi: C. C then.' stem: Patient involved in RTA with air in the chest and neck/ after trauma. Most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: air in the chest and neck
why_right: After blunt chest trauma (RTA), "air in the chest and neck" means air has escaped from the lung into the pleural space (pneumothorax) and tracked into the soft tissues of the neck (subcutaneous emphysema). A rib fracture puncturing the lung is the commonest mechanism, so pneumothorax is the most likely diagnosis. Expect reduced breath sounds, hyperresonance and crepitus over the chest wall and neck.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aortic injury: deceleration injury that shows a widened mediastinum and hypotension, not free air in the chest and neck.
C. Pulmonary embolism: a clot in the pulmonary arteries causing sudden dyspnea and hypoxia, usually days after trauma or immobility; it never produces air in the tissues.
D. Cardiac contusion: blunt injury to the myocardium presenting with arrhythmias or ECG changes and troponin rise, not with air leak.
key_concept:
Air in the chest after trauma = pneumothorax until proven otherwise.
  • Air + crepitus in neck/chest wall = subcutaneous emphysema from lung leak
  • Tension: trachea shifted away, raised JVP, hypotension, hyperresonance
  • Tension treatment: needle decompression then chest tube
  • Simple pneumothorax treatment: chest tube
  • Persistent large air leak + pneumomediastinum: think tracheobronchial injury
exam_pearl: Air in tissues points to a leak from lung or airway; widened mediastinum points to the aorta; raised JVP with equal air entry points to tamponade.

stem: Following a head-on motor vehicle collision, a 21-year-old unrestrained passenger presents to ER with dyspnea and respiratory distress. She is intubated and physical examination reveals subcutaneous emphysema and decreased breath sounds. Chest x-ray reveals cervical emphysema, pneumomediastinum, and a right-sided pneumothorax. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A head-on (deceleration) collision with respiratory distress, subcutaneous and cervical emphysema, pneumomediastinum and a pneumothorax together is the classic picture of a tracheobronchial injury. The disrupted airway leaks air into the mediastinum, neck and pleura at the same time, usually near the carina. Clues that confirm it in practice are a persistent large air leak or a lung that fails to re-expand after a chest tube; bronchoscopy confirms the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tension pneumothorax: explains the pneumothorax but not the pneumomediastinum and cervical emphysema; it would show tracheal shift, raised JVP and hypotension.
B. Open pneumothorax: requires an open chest wall wound (sucking chest wound), which is absent after this blunt injury.
D. Esophageal injury: can also cause pneumomediastinum, but it is rare in blunt trauma and presents with chest pain, dysphagia and sepsis (or follows vomiting in Boerhaave), not immediate respiratory distress with pneumothorax.
E. Pulmonary contusion: bruised lung causing hypoxia with patchy opacities on X-ray; it does not cause free air in the mediastinum or neck.
key_concept:
Air everywhere (neck + mediastinum + pleura) after blunt deceleration = tracheobronchial injury.
  • Persistent air leak or non-expanding lung after chest tube = suspect airway tear
  • Diagnosis: bronchoscopy
  • Esophageal perforation: pneumomediastinum + chest pain/vomiting, contrast leak on esophagography
  • Tension pneumothorax: tracheal shift, raised JVP, hypotension
  • Open pneumothorax: chest wall defect
  • Pulmonary contusion: hypoxia + opacities, no free air
exam_pearl: Pneumothorax alone = lung leak; pneumothorax plus pneumomediastinum plus neck emphysema after blunt trauma = airway rupture.

stem: A patient came to the ER with multiple fractures and was given crystalloids but continued bleeding profusely. Labs showed Hb < 7 g/dL and severe tachycardia. The source of bleeding was not mentioned. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: The patient keeps bleeding profusely despite crystalloids, with Hb < 7 g/dL and severe tachycardia: a non-responder in hemorrhagic shock. Ongoing hemorrhage in an unstable trauma patient needs immediate operative control, and the abdomen is the commonest hidden source, so surgical laparotomy is the most appropriate next step among these options. Unstable patients go to the operating room, not to further tests or laparoscopy.
why_wrong_block:
A. ABG: may support the assessment of shock but does nothing to stop the bleeding and delays definitive control.
B. Diagnostic laparoscopy: reserved for stable patients with an unclear diagnosis; pneumoperitoneum worsens hemodynamics in shock and the view is poor with massive bleeding.
key_concept:
Unstable trauma patient with ongoing bleeding = control the hemorrhage surgically.
  • Non-responder to fluids = active bleeding, needs blood products + operative control
  • Stable patient: CT to define injuries
  • Unstable patient: laparotomy, never CT or laparoscopy
  • Pelvic fracture source: binder, then angioembolization or packing
  • Chest source: chest tube, thoracotomy if output criteria met
exam_pearl: Instability is the decision point: stable goes to the scanner, unstable goes to the operating room.

stem: Patient came complaining of bleeding with and after defecation with mild itching, what's the cause:
why_right: Bleeding with and after defecation without any mention of pain, plus mild itching, is the typical picture of internal hemorrhoids. They bleed bright red blood on the stool or paper and commonly cause pruritus and mucus discharge. The absence of sharp pain, swelling, fever or chronic discharge rules out the other options.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anal fissure: also bleeds bright red blood, but the key feature is sharp, severe pain during and after defecation, usually with constipation.
B. Perianal abscess: a painful, tender perianal swelling with fever and leukocytosis, not bleeding with stool.
D. Fistula: presents with persistent perianal discharge from an external opening, often after a previous abscess, not bleeding with defecation.
key_concept:
Anorectal complaint by its dominant symptom:
  • Painless bright red bleeding (± itching) = hemorrhoids
  • Painful bleeding on defecation = fissure (midline, 6 or 12 o'clock)
  • Painful swelling + fever + leukocytosis = abscess
  • Chronic discharge = fistula
  • Painful tender purplish lump = thrombosed external hemorrhoid
exam_pearl: Pain is the switch: the same bright red bleeding is a fissure if it hurts and hemorrhoids if it does not.

stem: A patient has a thyroid mass and laboratory results show a markedly elevated serum calcitonin level 48. This finding is most consistent with which type of thyroid cancer?
why_right: Calcitonin is made by the parafollicular C cells, and medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from these cells. A thyroid mass with an elevated serum calcitonin therefore points to medullary carcinoma, and calcitonin (with CEA) is also its tumor marker for follow-up. Treatment is total thyroidectomy, and MEN 2 (RET mutation) should be considered.
why_wrong_block:
A. Papillary carcinoma: arises from follicular cells, spreads by lymphatics to cervical nodes, and is followed with thyroglobulin, not calcitonin.
B. Follicular carcinoma: also a follicular cell tumor followed with thyroglobulin; it spreads hematogenously to bone, lung and liver.
D. Anaplastic carcinoma: a rapidly growing hard mass in an elderly patient with compressive symptoms; it is not a calcitonin secreting tumor.
key_concept:
Match the thyroid cancer to its cell and marker:
  • Medullary: C cells, calcitonin (and CEA), MEN 2/RET, total thyroidectomy
  • Papillary: follicular cells, lymphatic spread, thyroglobulin
  • Follicular: follicular cells, hematogenous spread, thyroglobulin
  • Anaplastic: elderly, rapid growth, compression, poor prognosis
  • Hashimoto + rapidly enlarging goiter: think thyroid lymphoma
exam_pearl: Calcitonin = medullary; thyroglobulin = papillary or follicular.

stem: A 30 year old male presented with foul smelling of perianal discharge. No change in bowel habits, no bleeding no diarrhea. On examination, 3 perianal fistulas were found on 7 and 3 o'clock and maybe 11 o'clock. What is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: No change in bowel habits, no bleeding no diarrhea
why_right: This recall's key is pelvic MRI because the patient has multiple perianal fistulas (3 openings) with foul discharge, which makes them complex fistulas. Pelvic MRI is the imaging of choice to map complex tracts, their relation to the sphincters and any hidden abscess before surgery. Multiple fistulas in a young adult should also raise suspicion of Crohn's disease.
why_wrong_block:
B. Fistulogram: an outdated contrast study that poorly shows tracts in relation to the sphincters; it has been replaced by MRI.
C. Rectal US: endoanal ultrasound is an acceptable alternative where MRI is unavailable, but it is operator dependent and less accurate for complex or high tracts.
D. Colonoscopy: used to look for underlying Crohn's disease when complex fistulas occur without a known diagnosis; it does not map the fistula tracts themselves.
key_concept:
Simple vs complex perianal fistula:
  • Simple low fistula: fistulotomy
  • Complex (multiple, recurrent, high): image the tracts with pelvic MRI
  • Known Crohn's + complex fistula: MRI to assess the tract
  • Crohn's not known: colonoscopy to confirm Crohn's
  • Then antibiotics; infliximab for refractory Crohn's fistulas
exam_pearl: Multiple or recurrent fistulas are complex and possibly Crohn's: MRI maps the tract, colonoscopy looks for the cause.

stem: 28-year-old patient presented to the clinic complaining of perianal discharge. He reported history of on-off abdominal pain. He reported family history of Crohn's disease. On examination, three fistula openings at 3, 7 and 9 o'clock. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 28-year-old with "three fistula openings", recurrent abdominal pain and a family history of Crohn's has multiple, complex perianal fistulae that point to undiagnosed Crohn's disease. This recall's key is colonoscopy (with ileoscopy and biopsies) to confirm the underlying disease, because fistula management is very different in Crohn's (medical therapy, setons, avoiding fistulotomy).
why_wrong_block:
B. MRI: the gold-standard imaging to map fistula tracts and find abscesses; it is the answer when Crohn's is already known and the question asks for fistula anatomy or a suspected abscess.
C. Fistulogram: an older, less accurate way to outline a tract, largely replaced by MRI and endoanal ultrasound.
D. US: endoanal ultrasound can assess simple tracts and sphincters, but transabdominal US does not diagnose Crohn's or map complex perianal disease.
key_concept:
Multiple or recurrent perianal fistulae: think Crohn's.
  • Suspected Crohn's not yet diagnosed: colonoscopy with ileoscopy and biopsy
  • Fistula anatomy or abscess: MRI pelvis
  • Abscess: drain before escalating immunosuppression
  • Fistulizing Crohn's: anti-TNF (infliximab), setons
  • Simple low non-Crohn's fistula: fistulotomy
exam_pearl: Known Crohn's with perianal sepsis: MRI pelvis; suspected but undiagnosed Crohn's: colonoscopy.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0013).
Compiler note: 'Q:' variant under 2100 with a different stem (abdominal pain, family history of Crohn's); compiler highlighted Colonoscopy.

stem: crohns disease, presented with distended bowel, but no bleeding or diarrhea (I think that's how it's written), on imaging it shows a large distended bowl (not abscess). What's the management:
key_concept:
Crohn's complication decides the management:
  • Abscess: percutaneous drainage + antibiotics
  • Stricture with obstruction (vomiting, pain, distension): resection, stricturoplasty second line
  • Uncomplicated obstruction: start with bowel rest, NG decompression, IV fluids
  • Strangulation, perforation or instability: laparotomy
  • Perianal fistula: MRI, antibiotics, biologics
exam_pearl: No abscess on imaging removes drainage; distended bowel makes this an obstruction (stricture) question.

stem: An 80-year-old man presents with lower abdominal pain. He is afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal ultrasound reveals a 1 × 1 cm fluid collection in the lower abdomen. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptB: Start empiric IV antibiotics and observe
key_concept:
Intra-abdominal collection ladder:
  • Small (below 4 × 4 cm), stable: antibiotics (conservative)
  • 4 × 4 cm or more: percutaneous (image-guided) drainage
  • Multiple collections: laparoscopy
  • Unstable patient: laparotomy
exam_pearl: Size and stability drive the choice: a 1 cm collection is never drained first.

Compiler note: No answer marked for 2106; the following item 2107 (febrile version) has Answer: B.
