stem: Adult involved in MVA with irregular breathing low bp and pulse (cushing's triad) but oriented and cannt move his limbs what to do?
why_right: A conscious patient who "cannot move his limbs" after an MVA with irregular/shallow breathing has a high cervical cord injury with impending respiratory failure, so the airway must be secured. The method of choice is orotracheal intubation (rapid sequence) with manual in-line stabilisation of the neck; a suspected C-spine injury is not a contraindication. Low BP with a slow pulse here reflects neurogenic shock.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tracheostomy: a planned procedure for prolonged ventilation (common later in high cord injury), not an emergency airway.
B. Cricothyroidotomy: the emergency surgical airway when orotracheal intubation fails or is impossible, e.g. severe maxillofacial injury or profuse oral bleeding; not first line here.
D. Nasotracheal tube: less reliable, needs spontaneous breathing, and is contraindicated with midface or basal skull fractures; it is not the preferred trauma airway.
key_concept:
Trauma airway: orotracheal intubation with in-line stabilisation is the default.
  • Intubate for: SpO2 below 88%, GCS 8 or less, aspiration risk, high cord injury with failing breathing
  • Facial/mandibular fracture or failed intubation: cricothyroidotomy
  • Tracheostomy: later, for prolonged ventilation
  • Cushing triad (raised ICP) = hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing; hypotension + bradycardia after cord injury = neurogenic shock
exam_pearl: C-spine injury does not push you to a surgical airway: intubate orally with manual in-line stabilisation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Options and Answer: C on p589. Compiler's 'Q:' restatement (same question, same options, Answer: C): A trauma patient presents with quadriplegia (unable to move arms and legs), is conscious and oriented, but has shallow breathing. What is the best method to secure the airway? A. Tracheostomy B. Cricothyrotomy C. Orotracheal intubation D. Nasotracheal intubation.

stem: Post MVA pt was hypotensive and tachycardic, ct scan was done and showed “large internal pelvic hematoma actively bleeding” most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: large internal pelvic hematoma actively bleeding
why_right: The patient is in haemorrhagic shock ("hypotensive and tachycardic") from an "actively bleeding" pelvic hematoma, so the immediate priority is circulation: restore volume with blood products (massive transfusion protocol) while the pelvis is stabilised. Pelvic bleeding is retroperitoneal, so it is controlled by a pelvic binder, angioembolization or preperitoneal packing, not by opening the peritoneal cavity. Of the two options, transfusion is the correct management.
why_wrong_block: A. Ex lap does not reach a retroperitoneal pelvic bleed and opening the abdomen can release the tamponade and worsen the bleeding. It is right when the unstable trauma patient has intraperitoneal bleeding (positive FAST / free intraperitoneal blood).
key_concept:
Unstable pelvic bleeding: resuscitate and control the pelvis, do not laparotomise.
  • Circulation first: large-bore access, blood products (balanced transfusion)
  • Pelvic binder to close the pelvic volume
  • Arterial bleed on CT (contrast blush): angioembolization
  • Venous / unstable and no angio: preperitoneal packing ± external fixation
  • Positive FAST + unstable: laparotomy is for the abdomen, not the pelvis
exam_pearl: Pelvic hematoma = retroperitoneal: binder and embolization, not ex lap; free intraperitoneal blood in an unstable patient = ex lap.

stem: 40-50? year-old man undergoes colonoscopy, which reveals a 1.5 cm polyp in the colon Histopathology: Tubular Adenoma found and removed completely. When should the next colonoscopy screening be performed?
why_right: A tubular adenoma of "1.5 cm" is 10 mm or larger, which makes it an advanced adenoma (size alone qualifies, even with tubular histology). After complete removal of an advanced adenoma, surveillance colonoscopy is repeated at 3 years. The "removed completely" clue rules out an early re-look for incomplete resection.
why_wrong_block:
A. 3 to 6 months is for a large polyp removed piecemeal or incompletely, to check the resection site; here it was removed completely.
C. 10 years is the interval after a normal colonoscopy (average-risk screening) or for small hyperplastic polyps, not after an advanced adenoma.
D. An adenoma is a premalignant lesion, so surveillance is always needed; stopping screening is never right after an adenoma in a man of this age.
key_concept:
Post-polypectomy interval depends on size, number and histology.
  • Normal colonoscopy: 10 years
  • Small hyperplastic polyps: 10 years
  • 1 to 2 small tubular adenomas (<10 mm): 7 to 10 years
  • Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous component or high-grade dysplasia: 3 years
  • Piecemeal removal of a large polyp: 6 months
  • Malignant risk: villous > tubulovillous > tubular > hyperplastic
exam_pearl: Size ≥1 cm makes even a tubular adenoma "advanced": 3 years, not 10.

stem: A guy with severe perineal pain and swelling, discoloration that is expanding with crepitus, what is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Severe perineal pain with swelling, skin "discoloration that is expanding" and "crepitus" is necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia, i.e. Fournier's gangrene. Crepitus reflects gas from polymicrobial (including anaerobic) infection in the deep tissues, and rapid spread with violaceous skin marks necrosis. It is a surgical emergency treated with urgent debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cellulitis gives redness, warmth and pain after minor trauma but no crepitus and no rapidly spreading dusky discoloration; pain out of proportion plus crepitus means necrotizing infection.
B. Testicular torsion presents with sudden testicular pain, a high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex, usually in an adolescent; it does not cause perineal crepitus or spreading skin necrosis.
key_concept:
Perineal pain + spreading discoloration + crepitus = Fournier gangrene.
  • Necrotizing fasciitis of perineum, scrotum/penis (labia in females)
  • Polymicrobial: gram positive, gram negative, anaerobes
  • Clues: pain out of proportion, crepitus, bullae, violaceous skin, systemic toxicity
  • Treatment: urgent surgical debridement + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
  • Untreated mortality is high
exam_pearl: Crepitus is the word that converts "cellulitis" into necrotizing infection needing the theatre.

stem: A 14-year-old patient presented with a painless neck swelling. Examination confirmed a midline neck swelling below the hyoid bone that moves up and down with swallowing. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: midline neck swelling below the hyoid bone
moves up and down with swallowing
why_right: A painless "midline" swelling "below the hyoid" that "moves up and down with swallowing" in a young patient is a thyroglossal cyst. It arises from a remnant of the thyroglossal duct, which is attached to the hyoid, so it moves with swallowing and classically also with tongue protrusion. Treatment is surgical excision (Sistrunk operation, including the central hyoid).
why_wrong_block:
A. Cystic hygroma is a lateral (posterior triangle) soft, transilluminating lymphatic mass, usually seen in infancy; it is not midline and does not move with swallowing.
C. A midline dermoid cyst is also midline but is not attached to the hyoid, so it does not move with swallowing or tongue protrusion; it is often more superficial or submental.
D. Submental lymph nodes lie above the hyoid, are often tender when reactive and do not move with swallowing.
key_concept:
Midline neck mass: does it move with swallowing / tongue protrusion?
  • Moves with tongue protrusion and swallowing, at/below hyoid: thyroglossal cyst
  • Moves with swallowing only: thyroid nodule / goiter
  • Midline, no movement: dermoid cyst
  • Lateral, transilluminates, infant: cystic hygroma
  • Lateral, anterior to SCM: branchial cyst
exam_pearl: Movement with TONGUE PROTRUSION separates thyroglossal cyst from a thyroid nodule, which moves only with swallowing.

stem: Acute mesenteric ischemia history of ischemic stroke 1 month ago what is the initial management ?
why_right: The lead-in asks for the "initial management" of acute mesenteric ischemia. The first step is resuscitation and anticoagulation: IV fluids for the third-space losses and IV unfractionated heparin to stop clot propagation, before imaging (CT angiography) and revascularization. The "ischemic stroke 1 month ago" also points to an embolic source and contraindicates thrombolysis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Angiography with embolectomy is the definitive treatment for embolic mesenteric ischemia, but it follows resuscitation and heparin; it is not the initial step.
B. Thrombolysis is contraindicated here because of an ischemic stroke within the last 3 months, and it is not the first step anyway; catheter-directed lysis is reserved for selected early cases without peritonitis.
D. Abdominal ultrasound is limited by bowel gas and does not show the mesenteric vessels adequately; CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice.
key_concept:
Acute mesenteric ischemia: resuscitate, anticoagulate, image, revascularize.
  • Clue: elderly, AF/MI/recent embolic event, pain out of proportion to exam
  • Labs: leukocytosis, lactic acidosis
  • Initial: IV fluids + IV heparin (+ broad-spectrum antibiotics)
  • Diagnosis: CT angiography
  • Embolus: embolectomy; peritonitis/infarcted bowel: laparotomy + resection
exam_pearl: "Initial" = fluids and heparin; "definitive" = embolectomy. Recent stroke excludes thrombolysis.

stem: Patient arrived to ER after head injury, upon Glasgow Coma Scale calculation, he can open eyes to painful stimuli, localizes the pain and says groaning sounds only, what is the calculated GCS for him?
why_right: Score each component: eyes open "to painful stimuli" = E2; "localizes the pain" = M5; "groaning sounds only" = incomprehensible sounds = V2. Total GCS = 2 + 5 + 2 = 9.
why_wrong_block:
A. 8 would require motor 4 (withdrawal from pain) instead of localizing, or one point less elsewhere; localizing to pain is motor 5.
C. 10 would need inappropriate words (V3) or eye opening to speech (E3); groaning is V2 and opening to pain is E2.
D. 11 overscores by two points, e.g. it would need both eyes to speech and words rather than sounds.
key_concept:
GCS = Eyes (4) + Verbal (5) + Motor (6), range 3 to 15.
  • Eyes: 4 spontaneous, 3 to speech, 2 to pain, 1 none
  • Verbal: 5 oriented, 4 confused, 3 inappropriate words, 2 incomprehensible sounds, 1 none
  • Motor: 6 obeys, 5 localizes, 4 withdraws, 3 abnormal flexion, 2 extension, 1 none
  • GCS ≤8: intubate
exam_pearl: Localizes (hand moves to the stimulus) = M5; withdraws (pulls away) = M4. Groaning = V2.

stem: Patient in 60s diagnosed with prostate cancer presenting with back pain, urine retention and maybe lower limb weakness. What is the Appropriate Next Step:
OptD: Oral analgesia and reassess after 24 hours
why_right: Prostate cancer most often metastasises to the spine, and "back pain, urine retention" with "lower limb weakness" means metastatic spinal cord compression, an oncological emergency. The next step is immediate high-dose IV dexamethasone to reduce cord edema, together with urgent whole-spine MRI and then radiotherapy or surgical decompression. Delay risks permanent paralysis and sphincter loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Physiotherapy is for mechanical back pain or rehabilitation after decompression; it delays treatment of a cord compression.
B. MRI is the right test but it must be urgent (same day), not outpatient; outpatient imaging is for back pain without red flags or neurological deficit.
D. Analgesia and reassessing after 24 hours wastes the window to save neurological function; that approach suits simple back pain without red flags.
key_concept:
Known cancer + back pain + neuro deficit/retention = cord compression until proven otherwise.
  • Common primaries: prostate, breast, lung
  • Step 1: high-dose IV dexamethasone
  • Step 2: urgent whole-spine MRI
  • Definitive: radiotherapy or surgical decompression
  • Late signs: urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, leg weakness
exam_pearl: "Outpatient MRI" is the trap: right test, wrong urgency.

stem: A 71 years old man known IHD, complaining of severe central abdominal pain for 10 hours, and vomit 3 times; on examination there was mild tenderness, there mild bowl sluggish. Amylase 400 and WBC 22K.
why_right: An elderly man with "IHD" (cardiovascular embolic/thrombotic risk) has "severe" central abdominal pain but only "mild tenderness": pain out of proportion to examination, the hallmark of acute mesenteric ischemia. Marked leukocytosis ("WBC 22K") reflects bowel ischemia, and sluggish bowel sounds suggest evolving ileus. Amylase is often moderately raised in bowel ischemia, so it does not make this pancreatitis.
why_wrong_block: B. Acute pancreatitis gives epigastric pain radiating to the back with clear epigastric tenderness and a risk factor such as gallstones or alcohol; it is chosen when amylase/lipase is ≥3 times the upper limit with characteristic pain. Here the cardiac history and pain out of proportion favour ischemia.
key_concept:
Old + cardiac disease + severe pain, soft abdomen = mesenteric ischemia.
  • Leukocytosis and lactic acidosis support ischemia
  • Amylase can rise in ischemic bowel: not specific for pancreatitis
  • Pancreatitis = 2 of 3: typical pain, enzymes ≥3x ULN, imaging
  • Confirm ischemia with CT angiography
exam_pearl: A raised amylase does not equal pancreatitis; the cardiac patient with pain out of proportion is ischemia.

stem: 46-year-old woman undergoes a routine screening mammogram, reported as completely normal. She has no symptoms and no family history. When should she do her next mammogram?
highlight_terms_source: screening mammogram, reported as completely normal
why_right: This recall's key is annual screening because she is "46" with a normal mammogram, no symptoms and no family history, i.e. average risk in the 40 to 50 age band, where the taught schedule is yearly mammography. From 50 to 74 the interval lengthens to every 2 years, which is why the same scenario in a woman above 50 is keyed to 2 years.
why_wrong_block:
A. 6 months is a short-interval follow-up for a probably benign finding (BI-RADS 3), not for a completely normal screening mammogram.
C. 2 years is the interval taught for average-risk women aged 50 to 74 (and some guidelines apply it from 40); in this card's 40 to 50 rule the answer is yearly.
D. 3 years is not a mammography interval; it is the Pap smear (cytology) interval for cervical screening.
key_concept:
Mammography interval by age (average risk).
  • 40 to 50: yearly (this card's rule)
  • 50 to 74: every 2 years
  • BI-RADS 3: short-interval follow-up at 6 months
  • Pap cytology: every 3 years (do not confuse)
exam_pearl: Age decides it: under 50 yearly, 50 and above every 2 years.
compiler_note: Compiler note: "Above 50 → C. 2 years"

stem: A mechanic had an accidental injection of oil dissolving in his index finger. The finger is red and swollen with mild tenderness and normal joint movement. What to give??
why_right: An accidental injection of oil/solvent into the finger is a high-pressure injection injury, a surgical emergency even when the finger looks benign ("mild tenderness and normal joint movement"). The injected material tracks along tendon sheaths and fascial planes, causing chemical inflammation, ischemia and necrosis, so the finger needs urgent surgical exploration, decompression and debridement (drainage) of the foreign material. Delay greatly increases the risk of amputation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotics alone do not remove the injected material; they are an adjunct given alongside surgery. Antibiotics alone fit simple cellulitis without a retained injected substance.
B. Antibiotics and steroids are sometimes used as adjuncts after surgical debridement, but neither removes the oil, so they cannot replace surgery.
D. Elevation and ice is for a minor soft tissue contusion or sprain; it gives false reassurance and lets necrosis progress in an injection injury.
key_concept:
High-pressure injection injury (paint, grease, oil, solvent) = emergency surgical debridement.
  • Typical: worker with grease or paint gun, index finger of the non-dominant hand
  • Small entry wound, deceptively mild early exam
  • Organic solvents/paint are more destructive than grease
  • Treatment: urgent exploration, decompression, debridement + antibiotics
  • Delay → amputation
exam_pearl: A tiny wound and a normal-looking finger are the trap: injection injury always goes to theatre.

stem: Developed large neck swelling on the left side. On exam it is large 10 cm in size, US FNA showed clear lymphatic fluid. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: A large lateral (left) neck swelling in a young child with "clear lymphatic fluid" on aspiration is a cystic hygroma (macrocystic lymphatic malformation). It is benign, so the aim is removal or ablation of the malformation; of the listed options only surgery treats it, and excision is the definitive option for a large 10 cm lesion.
why_wrong_block:
B. Observation is not appropriate for a large 10 cm lesion, which risks airway compression, infection and hemorrhage into the cyst; spontaneous regression is uncommon.
C. Chemotherapy is for malignancy (e.g. lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma); clear lymphatic fluid indicates a benign malformation.
D. Radiotherapy has no role in a benign lymphatic malformation in a child and carries growth and malignancy risks.
key_concept:
Pediatric neck masses:
  • Midline, moves with tongue protrusion: thyroglossal cyst, excision (Sistrunk)
  • Anterior border of sternocleidomastoid: branchial cyst, excision
  • Lateral / posterior triangle, soft, transilluminates, clear lymph fluid: cystic hygroma, sclerotherapy then surgery
  • Hard, fixed, systemic symptoms: think malignancy, biopsy
exam_pearl: Clear lymphatic fluid in a lateral neck mass = cystic hygroma; if sclerotherapy is offered, it is usually first for macrocystic lesions.
compiler_note: Compiler note: No Sclerotherapy (among the options).

stem: Patient came to ER after he loss concious; after he regained it he experience sever headache describing it as worse headache he ever had. Plain CT showed: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage and Hydrocephalus. How are you going to investigate the affected artery?
why_right: The diagnosis is already made: "worst headache ever" after collapse, and plain CT shows SAH with hydrocephalus. The question now is "investigate the affected artery", i.e. find the bleeding aneurysm or vascular anomaly. Once CT confirms SAH, the next step is CT angiography, which is fast, noninvasive and shows the aneurysm to plan coiling or clipping.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI with contrast is slower, harder in a sick patient with hydrocephalus and less sensitive for acute blood; MR angiography is an alternative mainly when CT contrast is not possible, not the standard first vessel study.
B. Lumbar puncture only confirms SAH (xanthochromia, persistent RBCs) when CT is negative and more than 6 hours from onset; here CT is already positive and LP gives no information about the artery.
D. Transcranial Doppler is used after SAH to monitor for vasospasm, not to locate the ruptured aneurysm.
key_concept:
Thunderclap headache workup: confirm the bleed, then image the vessels.
  • Step 1: noncontrast CT head
  • CT positive for SAH: CT angiography to define the aneurysm
  • CT negative within 6 h of onset: SAH ruled out, look for other causes
  • CT negative after 6 h: lumbar puncture (xanthochromia, RBCs not clearing tube 1 to 4)
  • Abnormal LP: CT angiography
  • Digital subtraction angiography: gold standard if CTA is negative or for intervention
exam_pearl: "Diagnose SAH" with negative late CT = LP; "find the artery" after positive CT = CT angiography.

stem: RTA with dull percussion on exam and chest tube was inserted, Which of the following is an indication for surgical intervention?
why_right: Dull percussion after an RTA means hemothorax, and the chest tube both treats it and measures the bleeding. Thoracotomy is indicated when the tube shows major bleeding: a large initial output or continued drainage of about 200 ml/hr over several hours. Of the listed options only the ongoing 200 ml/hr output matches a recognised criterion.
why_wrong_block:
A. 500 ml initially is far below the threshold; the immediate output that mandates thoracotomy is more than 1500 ml.
C. Hemopneumothorax is managed with the same chest tube; the presence of air plus blood is not itself an indication for surgery.
D. Some drop in Hb and hematocrit is expected with any hemothorax and resuscitation; the trigger is chest tube output or hemodynamic decompensation, not a lab change alone.
key_concept:
Hemothorax: chest tube first, thoracotomy if the tube shows major bleeding.
  • Initial output more than 1500 ml
  • Ongoing output 200 to 300 ml/hr for several (classically 4) hours
  • Decompensation after initial stabilisation
  • Unstable patient: decision is by tube output, not CT
exam_pearl: The immediate threshold is 1500 ml, not 500 ml; smaller numbers are distractors.

stem: MVA patient with hemothorax managed by thoracostomy (chest tube). What's the indication of thoracotomy?
why_right: After a chest tube for traumatic hemothorax, thoracotomy is indicated by the volume and rate of bleeding. Persistent drainage of about 200 ml/hr for 4 hours means ongoing bleeding that the tube cannot control, so it is a classic criterion for thoracotomy.
why_wrong_block: B. An initial 500 ml is a moderate hemothorax that the chest tube alone usually manages; the immediate criterion is more than 1500 ml.
key_concept:
Indications for thoracotomy after chest tube in hemothorax:
  • Initial drainage more than 1500 ml
  • 200 to 300 ml/hr for 4 hours
  • Hemodynamic decompensation after initial stabilisation
exam_pearl: Two routes to thoracotomy: one big dump (more than 1500 ml) or a steady leak (200 ml/hr for 4 h).

stem: After accident a patient came with warm lower extremities with normal chest exam , BP was low, HR70 what kind of shock?
why_right: Trauma with low BP but HR 70 (no reflex tachycardia) and warm lower extremities points to neurogenic shock. Spinal cord injury cuts sympathetic outflow, causing vasodilation (warm skin) and unopposed vagal tone (normal or slow pulse). The normal chest exam also argues against tension pneumothorax or tamponade.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypovolemic shock causes vasoconstriction with cold, clammy extremities and tachycardia; it would be the answer if the patient were cold and tachycardic after trauma.
C. Cardiogenic or obstructive shock gives cold peripheries, tachycardia and cardiac signs such as raised JVP or muffled heart sounds, none of which are present.
D. Septic shock is also warm, but needs an infective source and produces tachycardia; it does not appear immediately after an accident.
key_concept:
Shock type by skin temperature and heart rate:
  • Cold + tachycardia: hypovolemic or cardiogenic
  • Warm + tachycardia: septic
  • Warm + normal or slow HR after trauma: neurogenic
  • Only cardiogenic has raised PCWP; only septic has raised cardiac output
exam_pearl: Hypotension without tachycardia after trauma = think spinal cord (neurogenic), but still exclude bleeding.

stem: Man had a car accident and he had “ interval consciousness” he was okay for 6 hours and get drowsy all over again
why_right: Head trauma, a period of being "okay" (the lucid interval), then deterioration to drowsiness is the classic picture of extradural (epidural) hemorrhage. It usually follows a temporal bone fracture tearing the middle meningeal artery; the arterial bleed expands after the initial concussion wears off and then compresses the brain.
why_wrong_block:
A. Subarachnoid hemorrhage presents with sudden severe headache and meningism (traumatic or aneurysmal), not a typical lucid interval followed by decline.
B. Subdural hematoma comes from torn bridging veins, typically in elderly or alcoholic patients, with a more gradual course; it can have delayed symptoms, but the lucid interval is the hallmark of extradural bleeding.
key_concept:
Extradural vs subdural:
  • Extradural: middle meningeal artery, temporal fracture, lucid interval, biconvex (lens) on CT
  • Subdural: bridging veins, elderly or alcoholics, crescent shaped on CT
  • Extradural with deterioration: urgent craniotomy and evacuation
exam_pearl: "Talked and then deteriorated" after head injury = extradural hematoma until proven otherwise.

stem: A diabetic patient presents with an ulcer over the lateral border of the foot. Which type of diabetic foot ulcer is most likely?
why_right: In a diabetic foot, the commonest ulcer is neuropathic: loss of protective sensation lets repeated pressure over bony points of the foot break the skin unnoticed. An ulcer on the border of the foot in a diabetic with no mention of ischemic signs is therefore read as neuropathic.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ischemic ulcers are painful, punched out with a pale or necrotic base, with cold foot and absent pulses; the stem gives no ischemic features (pulses decide this).
C. Venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area above the ankle (usually medial malleolus) with varicosities, edema and pigmentation, not on the border of the foot.
D. "Pressure ulcer" in the usual sense means a decubitus ulcer in an immobile patient (sacrum, heel); in a walking diabetic, pressure ulcers of the foot are classified as neuropathic.
key_concept:
Diabetic foot ulcer type: check sensation and pulses.
  • Neuropathic: painless, over pressure points (plantar metatarsal heads, toes), surrounding callus, warm foot, pulses present
  • Ischemic or neuroischemic: painful, margins of the foot (e.g. lateral border over the 5th metatarsal head), toe tips, heel, cold foot, weak or absent pulses
  • Neuroischemic (both features) is common in diabetics
  • Venous: gaiter region, edema, pigmentation, granulating base
exam_pearl: Same site, absent pulses and pain = ischemic; always let the pulse exam flip the answer.

stem: A diabetic patient presents with an ulcer with granulation in its center over the left lateral border of the foot (Not mentioned in scenario if ankle or leg). Left dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are intact. Which type of diabetic foot ulcer is most likely?
highlight_terms_source: dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are intact
why_right: Three clues give a neuropathic ulcer: the patient is diabetic, the ulcer is on the lateral border of the foot (a pressure point), and dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are intact, which excludes significant ischemia. The granulating centre shows a well perfused bed, typical of a neuropathic ulcer.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ischemic ulcers come with absent or weak pulses, pain and a pale or necrotic base; palpable distal pulses here argue strongly against them.
C. Venous ulcers also have intact pulses and a granulating base, but they sit in the gaiter region of the leg with edema and pigmentation, not on the foot border of a diabetic.
D. Pressure (decubitus) ulcers occur over the sacrum or heels in immobile patients; a diabetic foot ulcer at a weight bearing point is classified as neuropathic.
key_concept:
Ulcer approach: site + pulses + base.
  • Diabetic, pressure point, pulses present, granulating base: neuropathic
  • Absent pulses, punched out, necrotic base, painful: ischemic
  • Gaiter region, intact pulses, shallow irregular, pigmented skin: venous
exam_pearl: Intact pulses rule out ischemic; then the site (foot vs gaiter) separates neuropathic from venous.

stem: Patient post inguinal surgery. Incision site reveals erythema and seropurulent discharge. What is the diagnosis?
key_concept:
Surgical site infection by depth:
  • Superficial: skin and subcutaneous tissue, discharge from the incision
  • Deep: fascia and muscle, deep pus, dehiscence or abscess
  • Organ or space: collection in the operated space
  • Management: open the wound and drain; antibiotics if cellulitis or systemic signs
  • Seroma: swelling without pain, fever or redness, common after hernia repair
exam_pearl: Discharge from the incision moves it from cellulitis to SSI; depth of tissue involved decides superficial vs deep.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Pediatric patient with history of trauma (or injury) presented with severe pain out of proportion to the visible area and crepitation. Febrile. Management?
why_right: Recent injury, pain out of proportion to the visible skin change, crepitation and fever mean a necrotizing soft tissue infection (necrotizing fasciitis or gas gangrene). This is a surgical emergency: urgent surgical consultation for early debridement plus broad spectrum IV antibiotics and resuscitation.
why_wrong_block: B. Oral antibiotics suit mild cellulitis without systemic signs; they cannot reach necrotic tissue and delay the debridement that determines survival here.
key_concept:
Necrotizing soft tissue infection:
  • Clues: pain out of proportion, crepitus, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, skin discoloration or bullae
  • Gas gangrene: crepitus and foul smell, often after contaminated wounds
  • Treatment: urgent surgical debridement + broad spectrum IV antibiotics
  • Do not wait for imaging if the clinical picture is clear
exam_pearl: Crepitus or pain out of proportion converts "cellulitis" into a surgical emergency.

stem: RTA, there is pelvic fracture, no hematoma?
key_concept:
Pelvic fracture in trauma:
  • Unstable: ATLS, pelvic binder, FAST, then angioembolization or packing
  • Stable: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
  • Urethral injury signs: blood at meatus, perineal hematoma, high riding prostate, unable to void
  • Signs present: retrograde urethrogram first, no Foley
  • Confirmed urethral injury: suprapubic catheter
exam_pearl: Hematoma or blood at the meatus is what triggers a retrograde urethrogram; without them, image the fracture.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Anal fissure 6 o'clock management?
why_right: A fissure at 6 o'clock is the classic posterior midline (typical) fissure. With no history of chronicity or failed treatment, management starts medically: a topical cream that relaxes the internal sphincter (calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem, or a nitrate), plus fibre, fluids, stool softeners and sitz baths. Most acute fissures heal on this regimen.
why_wrong_block: A. Sphincterotomy (lateral internal) is for a chronic fissure (over 6 weeks, sentinel tag, exposed sphincter fibres) that has failed medical therapy; it is not first line and carries a small incontinence risk.
key_concept:
Anal fissure: treat by duration, not by pain severity.
  • All fissures: fibre, fluids, stool softener, sitz baths
  • Acute (<6 weeks): topical diltiazem or nitrate (chemical sphincterotomy)
  • Chronic (>6 weeks) failing medical therapy: lateral internal sphincterotomy
  • Botulinum toxin: alternative for chronic fissure when surgery is to be avoided
  • Typical sites: posterior midline (6 o'clock), then anterior (12 o'clock)
exam_pearl: Surgery only flips to the answer when the stem says chronic, sentinel tag, or failed topical therapy.

stem: Anal fissure 7, 3 (o'clock) management?
key_concept:
Fissure site matters.
  • 6 o'clock (posterior midline): typical, most common
  • 12 o'clock (anterior midline): typical, more common in women (postpartum)
  • Lateral (e.g. 3 or 7 o'clock), multiple or painless: atypical; think Crohn's, TB, HIV, syphilis, carcinoma; examine under anaesthesia with biopsy
  • 3, 7, 11 o'clock are the classic positions of internal haemorrhoids, a common recall mix-up
  • Acute: topical cream; chronic failing medical therapy: sphincterotomy
exam_pearl: A lateral fissure is a red flag for a secondary cause; do not jump to sphincterotomy before excluding Crohn's or infection.

Compiler note: Unnumbered follow-on variant printed under 2523 ("-Anal fissure 7, 3, management?"); no answer marked.

stem: Elderly presents to the Emergency Department with bright blood with his stool; he is known for colonic polyp and hypertension. On Ex he is pale and tachycardic. Vitals: BP 160/90, HR: 128. What is the most appropriate initial?
OptC: Oral iron ( yes I am sure)
why_right: An elderly man with bright red rectal bleeding who is pale and tachycardic (HR 128) has significant blood loss. The lead-in asks for the initial step, and in any GI bleed with haemodynamic compromise that is ABC resuscitation: large-bore IV access, IV fluids and blood transfusion, then localisation of the source. The BP of 160/90 does not reassure, because he is a known hypertensive and tachycardia is the earlier sign of shock.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urgent colonoscopy is the diagnostic and therapeutic test for lower GI bleeding (polyp is a likely source), but only after resuscitation and bowel preparation; it is never the first step in a tachycardic patient.
B. CT (angiography) is used to localise active bleeding in a patient who keeps bleeding, after resuscitation has started; it does not replace volume and blood replacement.
C. Oral iron treats chronic iron deficiency anaemia in a stable outpatient; it does nothing for acute haemorrhage with tachycardia.
key_concept:
Any GI bleed: resuscitate first, then find the source.
  • Step 1: assess haemodynamics (HR, BP, pallor, postural drop)
  • Unstable: two large-bore IV lines, crystalloid, crossmatch and transfuse, correct anticoagulation
  • Lower GI bleed once stable: colonoscopy after preparation
  • Ongoing brisk bleed: CT angiography, then embolisation
  • Massive bright red bleed with shock: exclude an upper GI source with endoscopy
exam_pearl: A normal or high BP in a known hypertensive with HR 128 is still shock; 'initial' means resuscitation.

stem: A patient with recent rectal surgery comes to you with absent pulses up to the femoral area. How will you manage such a case?
highlight_terms_source: absent pulses up to the femoral area
why_right: This recall is the garbled version of a known question: after rectal surgery a patient develops a thrombosis extending up to the femoral level (DVT from popliteal to common femoral vein). For a postoperative DVT without contraindication, first-line treatment is therapeutic low molecular weight heparin, enoxaparin, which is then continued or bridged to oral anticoagulation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Unfractionated heparin is preferred when LMWH is unsuitable: severe renal impairment, very high bleeding risk needing rapid reversal, or acute arterial limb ischaemia. None of these is stated.
C. IVC filter is reserved for proximal DVT/PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (e.g. active bleeding) or for clot progression despite adequate anticoagulation.
D. Thrombolysis is contraindicated soon after major surgery and is kept for massive PE with shock or limb-threatening iliofemoral DVT, not routine DVT.
key_concept:
Postoperative VTE treatment ladder.
  • DVT or stable PE: LMWH (enoxaparin) first line
  • Renal failure: unfractionated heparin
  • Anticoagulation contraindicated: IVC filter
  • PE with shock: thrombolysis (recent surgery is a relative contraindication)
  • Acute arterial limb ischaemia: IV unfractionated heparin, then embolectomy or revascularisation
exam_pearl: If the stem truly means absent ARTERIAL pulses (cold, pale, painful limb), it is acute limb ischaemia and IV unfractionated heparin is the first step.

stem: 7-year-old child presents with recurrent tonsillitis (six episodes in the past year), snoring, mouth breathing during sleep, and has grade three tonsils. What is the most appropriate management option for this patient?
highlight_terms_source: recurrent tonsillitis (six episodes in the past year)
why_right: This 7-year-old has obstructive sleep-disordered breathing (snoring, mouth breathing during sleep) with grade 3 tonsils, plus recurrent tonsillitis (six episodes in one year). Six episodes alone falls just short of the strict Paradise threshold, but sleep-disordered breathing is both an independent indication and a modifying factor that favours surgery. In an otherwise healthy child whose large tonsils explain the symptoms, adenotonsillectomy is the most appropriate management and first-line treatment of paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea.
why_wrong_block:
A. Family counselling is part of any plan but does not treat obstruction or recurrent infection; it is the answer when no surgical criteria are met.
B. Stopping medication has no role; no drug is causing the problem, and repeated antibiotics are the reason surgery is considered.
D. A sleep study (polysomnography) is required before surgery when the child has comorbidities (obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial or neuromuscular disease) or when tonsil size and symptoms do not match; here the picture is clear-cut.
key_concept:
Paediatric tonsillectomy indications.
  • Recurrent throat infection (Paradise): ≥7 episodes in 1 year, ≥5/year for 2 years, or ≥3/year for 3 years
  • Obstructive sleep-disordered breathing with tonsillar hypertrophy
  • Peritonsillar abscess recurrence
  • Suspected malignancy (asymmetric tonsil)
  • PSG first only if comorbid or symptoms and exam disagree
exam_pearl: Snoring plus big tonsils in a healthy child: go to adenotonsillectomy; a sleep study comes first only when the case is unclear or the child is high risk.

stem: Female patient with Lt hearing loss and tinnitus, autophony with preserved stapedial reflex, on examination normal tympanic membrane, diagnosis.
key_concept:
Normal TM + hearing symptoms: use the reflex.
  • Otosclerosis: conductive loss, stapedial reflex ABSENT
  • Superior canal dehiscence: pseudo-conductive loss, reflex PRESERVED, supranormal bone conduction, Tullio sign
  • Patulous Eustachian tube: autophony with breathing sounds, positional relief, TM moves with breathing, hearing usually normal
  • Weber lateralises to the affected ear in conductive or third-window loss
exam_pearl: Air-bone gap with an intact stapedial reflex is not otosclerosis; think third-window lesion.

stem: Child was brought to the hospital after the teacher suspected hearing loss. Otoscopy showed an intact tympanic membrane with fluid behind it, and the child had no fever or pain. Mild hearing loss was confirmed. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Fluid behind an intact TM with no fever or pain is otitis media with effusion (OME), not acute otitis media. Most OME resolves spontaneously, so with mild hearing loss the initial plan is watchful waiting for 3 months with a repeat hearing assessment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amoxicillin is for acute otitis media (fever, otalgia, bulging red TM); antibiotics give no lasting benefit in OME, and here there is no fever or pain.
C. Grommets are for OME persisting ≥3 months with documented hearing loss or speech, learning or behavioural impact, or structural TM changes; it is too early here.
key_concept:
OME vs AOM.
  • AOM: acute, febrile, painful, bulging red TM: amoxicillin when indicated
  • OME: fluid without signs of infection, dull or retracted TM, reduced mobility
  • OME new: observe 3 months, repeat audiology
  • Persistent OME (≥3 months) with hearing loss: tympanostomy tubes
  • No role: antibiotics, steroids, decongestants, antihistamines
exam_pearl: No fever and no pain with fluid behind the drum is OME; the answer is wait 3 months, not antibiotics.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Restatement (school-aged child, fluid in middle ear, mild decrease in hearing, initial management) highlighted 'Wait 3 months and follow-up'. OME with mild hearing loss and no acute infection: initial step is observation; only persistent OME (>3 months) with hearing loss or functional problems -> grommets; antibiotics not used for asymptomatic OME. Refs: AAP OME guideline 2016 (observation up to 3 months if hearing loss <30 dB), NICE NG91, UpToDate.

stem: A 5-year-old child has *persistent* otitis media with effusion and conductive hearing loss. The hearing problem was first noticed by the teacher. Otoscopic exam shows a retracted tympanic membrane. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
key_concept:
OME decision fork.
  • New OME: observe 3 months, repeat audiology
  • Persistent ≥3 months + hearing loss: tympanostomy tubes
  • Retraction pocket or structural TM change: ENT referral, consider tubes
  • Hearing aids: alternative when surgery declined or unsuitable
exam_pearl: The word 'persistent' means the observation period is already over.

stem: 5 years old child with persistent otitis media with effusion and conductive hearing loss is for surgical consideration?
why_right: In a 5-year-old with persistent OME and conductive hearing loss, the surgical procedure of choice is insertion of tympanostomy tubes (grommets). The tube ventilates the middle ear, drains the effusion and restores hearing immediately while the Eustachian tube matures.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mastoidectomy is for cholesteatoma, coalescent mastoiditis or chronic suppurative disease, not uncomplicated effusion.
B. Adenoidectomy alone does not restore hearing immediately; guidelines allow it (with or without tubes) from about age 4 or with nasal obstruction or repeat surgery, but tubes remain the standard first operation for hearing loss from OME.
C. Myringotomy alone drains fluid but the incision heals within days and the effusion reaccumulates, so it is not recommended without a tube.
key_concept:
Surgery for OME.
  • Indication: OME ≥3 months with hearing loss, or school, speech or behaviour impact
  • First operation: tympanostomy tubes
  • Adenoidectomy: option from about age 4, mainly with tubes, at repeat surgery or with nasal obstruction
  • Myringotomy alone: not advised
  • Mastoidectomy: cholesteatoma or mastoiditis only
exam_pearl: 'Myringotomy alone' is the trap; without a tube the hole closes and the fluid returns.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Shown twice in the 388 block. Tympanostomy tubes indicated in OME persisting >=3 months with documented hearing loss or educational/behavioral impact (AAP 2016, NICE NG91, UpToDate).

stem: A child presents with reduced tympanic membrane movement, and the school report notes decreased hearing. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: Reduced TM movement with a school report of decreased hearing and no features of acute infection suggests otitis media with effusion. The initial step is to quantify the hearing loss with a formal audiology assessment (audiometry and tympanometry); this establishes the baseline that guides observation versus tubes.
why_wrong_block:
A. Decongestants and antihistamines have no proven benefit in OME and are not recommended.
B. Amoxicillin is for acute otitis media (fever, otalgia, bulging TM); there are no signs of acute infection here.
D. Tympanostomy tubes come later, for OME persisting ≥3 months with documented hearing loss; hearing must be measured first.
key_concept:
Child with suspected hearing loss.
  • Step 1: formal audiology (age-appropriate audiometry, tympanometry)
  • OME confirmed: observe 3 months, re-test
  • Persistent with hearing loss: grommets
  • Speech delay or learning difficulty: always test hearing
  • No role: antibiotics, decongestants, antihistamines, steroids
exam_pearl: Before any treatment for a 'hearing problem' at school, measure the hearing.

stem: A child presented to the OPD with persistent purulent nasal discharge and low grade fever for 12 days. On examination: No periorbital swelling or restricted EOM. There is tenderness on the frontal bone. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: Purulent nasal discharge with fever persisting for 12 days (beyond 10 days without improvement) plus frontal tenderness meets the clinical definition of acute bacterial sinusitis. There are no complication signs (no periorbital swelling, EOM not restricted), so the child is managed as an outpatient with first line oral amoxicillin. Diagnosis is clinical; no imaging is needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Supportive care alone fits viral rhinosinusitis, which typically improves within about 10 days; symptoms persisting past 10 days indicate bacterial infection that warrants antibiotics.
C. Intranasal steroids are an adjunct (mainly in allergic or chronic rhinosinusitis) and do not replace antibiotics for acute bacterial sinusitis in a child.
D. Sinus X-ray is not recommended; uncomplicated sinusitis is a clinical diagnosis, and imaging (contrast CT) is reserved for suspected orbital or intracranial complications.
key_concept:
Acute bacterial sinusitis in children is a clinical diagnosis; treat with amoxicillin if criteria are met.
  • Persistent: nasal discharge or daytime cough >10 days without improvement
  • Severe onset: high fever with purulent discharge for 3 or more consecutive days
  • Worsening (double sickening): new worsening after initial improvement
  • First line: amoxicillin; no response by 72 h: amoxicillin clavulanate
  • Periorbital swelling, restricted EOM, proptosis or neuro signs: contrast CT plus IV antibiotics
exam_pearl: Under 10 days with improving symptoms is viral (supportive); once eye signs appear the answer flips to contrast CT.

stem: A child present with 6 adenotonsillitis after starting kindergarten. mother reports snoring and mouth breathing. On examination there is grade 3 tonsils. What is the next step in management? No Mention Of Daytime Symptoms
why_right: The child has recurrent adenotonsillitis (6 episodes) plus snoring and mouth breathing with grade 3 tonsils, i.e. obstructive sleep disordered breathing from adenotonsillar hypertrophy. In an otherwise healthy child whose large tonsils match the snoring history, clinical diagnosis is enough and the next step is referral for adenotonsillectomy, which treats both problems. The note "no mention of daytime symptoms" signals there is no discordance that would require a sleep study first.
why_wrong_block: B. Polysomnography is the diagnostic test for OSA, but before pediatric tonsillectomy it is reserved for children with comorbidities (obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial or neuromuscular disease, sickle cell disease) or when tonsil size does not match the reported symptoms.
key_concept:
Child with snoring plus tonsillar hypertrophy: adenotonsillectomy is first line treatment.
  • Sleep study first: obesity, Down syndrome, craniofacial anomaly, neuromuscular disease, sickle cell disease
  • Sleep study first: small tonsils but significant symptoms (discordance)
  • Recurrent tonsillitis threshold (Paradise): ≥7 in 1 year, ≥5 per year for 2 years, ≥3 per year for 3 years
  • Fewer episodes and no obstruction: watchful waiting
exam_pearl: Adult with daytime sleepiness and snoring: sleep study; healthy child with big tonsils and snoring: refer for adenotonsillectomy.

stem: Child complaining of nasal purulent discharge, eye pain, periorbital swelling and severe headache. On examination there is frontal bone tenderness and restricted extraocular movements. What is the most appropriate?
OptD: Refer to ear, nose, and throat (ENT)
why_right: Sinusitis (purulent discharge, frontal tenderness) with periorbital swelling, eye pain and restricted extraocular movements means the infection has spread behind the septum: orbital cellulitis, a complication. Restricted, painful eye movement separates it from preseptal cellulitis. Severe headache also raises concern for intracranial spread. A contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits, sinuses (and brain if needed) is required urgently to look for a subperiosteal or orbital abscess, alongside IV antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral amoxicillin treats uncomplicated acute bacterial sinusitis; orbital involvement needs admission, IV antibiotics and imaging.
C. Reassurance is never appropriate with eye signs; orbital cellulitis can cause vision loss, cavernous sinus thrombosis or brain abscess.
D. ENT (and ophthalmology) input is needed, but the CT is what defines an abscess needing drainage and should not be delayed; referral alone is not the most appropriate step.
key_concept:
Sinusitis with eye signs = complication until proven otherwise: contrast CT plus IV antibiotics.
  • Preseptal: lid swelling, normal eye movement, no proptosis, normal vision
  • Orbital: proptosis, painful restricted EOM, reduced acuity or colour vision, RAPD
  • Orbital spread usually from ethmoid sinusitis
  • Abscess on CT or worsening vision: surgical drainage
  • Severe headache or neuro signs: include brain imaging
exam_pearl: Restricted or painful eye movement is the single sign that turns preseptal (oral antibiotics) into orbital cellulitis (CT and IV antibiotics).

stem: boy with bacterial sinusitis , started on amoxicillin, didn’t improve after 3 days , what to do ?
why_right: Acute bacterial sinusitis treated with amoxicillin that has not improved after 3 days (72 h) is treatment failure, most likely from a beta lactamase producing organism (H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis) or resistant pneumococcus. The next step is to switch to amoxicillin clavulanate (high dose) without imaging, as long as there are no complication signs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance and continuing the same drug is wrong once there is no improvement at 72 h; that defines failure of first line therapy.
B. ENT referral is for complications (orbital or intracranial), recurrent or chronic sinusitis, or failure of second line antibiotics; a single amoxicillin failure is handled by broadening the antibiotic.
key_concept:
Pediatric acute bacterial sinusitis ladder.
  • First line: amoxicillin (with or without clavulanate)
  • Worse or no better at 72 h: amoxicillin clavulanate, high dose
  • Penicillin allergy: options include a third generation cephalosporin or clindamycin based regimens
  • Failure of second line or complication signs: contrast CT and specialist referral
exam_pearl: No improvement at 72 h means change the antibiotic, not image; eye or neuro signs mean CT.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' variant: fever, stuffed nose, headaches, bacterial sinusitis with no improvement after 72 hrs of amoxicillin; options A Refer to ENT, B CT Sinuses, C change medication to Amoxicillin clavulanate for 10 days, D change diagnosis; Answer: C.

stem: pt with night cough, itchy eye, palate, and nose, darkining of the eyelid:
key_concept:
Rhinitis types by history.
  • Allergic: itching (eyes, nose, palate), sneezing, clear discharge, shiners, seasonal or perennial triggers; treat with intranasal steroid, antihistamine, allergen avoidance
  • Rhinitis medicamentosa: rebound congestion after prolonged topical decongestant; treat by stopping the decongestant plus intranasal steroid
  • Infective: purulent discharge, fever
  • Vasomotor: triggered by temperature, odours, no itch
exam_pearl: Itch plus allergic shiners = allergic rhinitis; congestion only, with a decongestant spray history = rhinitis medicamentosa.
